fatal.detail: The rewrite deleted the only qualifier that made C uniquely right, and option B is a mathematically valid decomposition of aggregate equity value, so the item is now double-keyed. In 'before' the stem pointed at one specific published decomposition ('The curriculum expresses the aggregate market value of equity, V_e, using three multiplicative components'), so 'which decomposition is it' had exactly one answer. The rewritten stem asks a free-standing factual question, 'The aggregate market value of equity in an economy is most likely expressed as the product of:', and under that stem B is true as written: aggregate book value x aggregate ROE = aggregate earnings, and aggregate earnings x aggregate P/E = aggregate market value of equity. That is an identity at any level of aggregation, not only at firm level. The after-rationale for B concedes the arithmetic ('Book value multiplied by return on equity gives earnings, and the P/E multiple capitalizes those earnings') and then rests the distinction entirely on a framing the stem no longer supplies ('It is not the aggregate market decomposition, which has to begin from the size of the economy rather than from a company's balance sheet') - a learner reading only the stem has no basis for preferring C. The citation did have to go under rule 9, but it needed replacing with a substantive restriction in the stem (e.g. asking for the decomposition that links aggregate equity value to the size of the economy), not simply dropping it.
fatal.quote_before: The curriculum expresses the aggregate market value of equity, V_e, using three multiplicative components. This decomposition is most likely: ... B: "V_e = Book value × Return on equity × P/E."
fatal.quote_after: The aggregate market value of equity in an economy is most likely expressed as the product of: ... B: "Book value, return on equity and the P/E multiple."

fatal.detail: The reframe cut the case anchor out of the stem and in doing so turned distractor B into a true statement. Before, the stem tied the question to one specific market ('In the Belvia case (Example 6), Dwight also faces high concentration risk in the equity market because most likely:'), so B was false as a matter of fact about that market — its rationale said only 'This is not the concentration described.' The rewritten stem asks a generic question, 'Concentration risk in a small emerging equity market most likely arises from:', and under that stem 'a single global technology company dominating the market' is a correct answer to it: one issuer dominating a market is concentration risk, and it is a more extreme concentration than the sector-plus-ownership mix in A. A and B now collide, with B defensible on the stem's own terms (a learner can point to Taiwan or Korea), so the item is no longer uniquely keyed to A. Nothing in the stem as rewritten lets the learner rule B out; only the vanished Belvia facts did that.
fatal.quote_before: STEM: "In the Belvia case (Example 6), Dwight also faces high concentration risk in the equity market because most likely:" / B: "The equity market is dominated by a single global technology company." / rationale B: "This is not the concentration described."
fatal.quote_after: STEM: "Concentration risk in a small emerging equity market most likely arises from:" / B: "a single global technology company dominating the market."

fatal.detail: Dropping the universal quantifier turned the B distractor into a defensible answer, so the item is now double-keyed against C. Before, B read 'Always overstate diversification benefits.' — false because of 'Always'. After, it reads 'overstate an asset's diversification value.', an unqualified statement under a stem that only asks what pairwise correlations 'are most likely to' do. The after-rationale for B concedes the direction does occur: 'Pairwise correlations can make a redundant asset appear diversifying', and defends B only with a qualifier that exists nowhere in the option text — 'they do not systematically overstate the benefit.' The sidebar example the key rests on (an asset that is an exact weighted combination of two holdings, adding no diversification value, yet showing only moderate pairwise correlations) is itself an overstatement of diversification value, so a learner reading B has a direct textual case for it. B is also now a strict subset of keyed C ('mismeasure an asset's diversification value.'): if B holds, C holds, so the two can no longer be separated without the rationale's unstated 'systematically'. Restoring 'always' (or 'systematically') to option B fixes it.
fatal.quote_before: Always overstate diversification benefits.
fatal.quote_after: overstate an asset's diversification value.

fatal.detail: The stem is unchanged: "Alternative weighting schemes to market-cap weighting for the global market portfolio most likely include:". Distractor B's only falsifier was the word "only" — it was false because it asserted trailing-earnings weighting was the sole alternative, which is exactly what the old rationale said: "Earnings-weighting alone is not identified." With "only" deleted, B now claims merely that trailing-earnings weighting is among the alternatives to market-value weighting, which is defensible (it is the standard fundamental-indexation alternative), so the stem's "include" is satisfied. The rewritten rationale had to abandon the original reason and substitute a new, weaker one — "not among the alternatives identified. It is a fundamental-indexation idea rather than one of the recognized substitutes" — which concedes it is a weighting scheme. Key A ("GDP weighting or equal weighting") is still the curriculum-named answer but is now only arguably better than B rather than uniquely correct.

fatal.quote_after: Trailing-earnings weighting.

fatal.detail: Same defect in the third option. "Book-value weighting only." was false because of "only", and the old rationale named that reason exactly: "Book value alone is not the identified alternative." Shortened to "Book-value weighting.", the option now asserts only that book-value weighting is one of the alternatives to market-cap weighting, which is true in the ordinary sense (book-value weighting is the canonical fundamental-index alternative). Like earnings weighting it is an accounting-based measure of size...", concedes it is a measure of size used for weighting, so it no longer establishes that the option is wrong. fatal.detail: The whole falsity of distractor A lived in its causal clause, and the rewrite deleted it. Before, A read "Capital preservation, because appraisal-based valuations give alternatives lower reported volatility than public equities." — false because it attributed capital preservation to appraisal smoothing. fatal.detail: The reframed stem inverts the direction of the swap position. 'Pays a fixed rate of 2.8535% against a six-month MRR of 0.5925%' is the standard idiom for a PAY-fixed swap, and it contradicts the 'receive-fixed' label in the same clause; the before-stem avoided this by stating the rate without an operative verb ('receive-fixed swap at 2.8535%, 6m MRR 0.5925%'). Read literally, carry is -GBP1,130,500 and the 50 bp fall in rates produces a mark-to-market loss (the rationale's own approximation, 8.318 x GBP100M / 10,000 x 50 = GBP4,159,000, flips sign), so the six-month gain is about -GBP5,364,760. Among the three options the closest value is then A (GBP100,000), distance GBP5,464,760, against GBP10,729,520 for the keyed C -- the item is mis-keyed on its literal reading, not merely ambiguous. Rationale C still reasons from the receive-fixed side ('Swap carry is GBP1,130,500 = [(2.8535% - 0.5925%)/2] x GBP100 million' and 'the swap mark-to-market gain is GBP4,234,260'), so stem and rationale now describe opposite positions. All other inputs the reframe needed are present; the fix is the verb alone.

fatal.detail: Entry 577 (key A). The distractor lost the one word that made it false. Before, C was a definitional claim — the stem read "The reading's butterfly strategy for curvature is most likely:" and C answered "uses bullet-only exposure concentrated at a single maturity point"; "bullet-only" is what made it wrong, because a butterfly is never bullet-only. After, the stem reads "A yield curve butterfly strategy for curvature most likely involves:" and C reads "Bullet exposure concentrated at a single maturity." With "only" deleted and the stem's verb changed from "is" to "involves", C is now a true statement about a butterfly: the intermediate-term bullet body IS exposure concentrated at a single maturity, so a butterfly does involve it. Key A ("A long bullet paired with a short barbell, or the reverse") remains the fuller and better answer, but C is no longer wrong, and the rationale confirms the mismatch: after-rationale C still argues against the deleted qualifier — "A bullet concentrated at a single maturity is only the body of the trade. Without the offsetting barbell wings there is no exposure to curvature" — i.e. it rebuts a claim the option no longer makes (option C as it now reads does not exclude the wings). fatal.detail: The rewrite replaced a three-word distractor rationale with invented arithmetic that is numerically false. Before, rationale C read in full: "Risk varies dramatically." After, it asserts that "the likelihood of credit loss at BB+ (940) is more than twice that at BBB- (610) and roughly eight times that at A- (180)." Neither ratio holds on the very factor table the item carries: 940/610 = 1.54, which is not more than twice, and 940/180 = 5.22, which is not roughly eight times. The figures themselves were preserved correctly from before (BBB- = 610, BB+ = 940, A- = 180, matching the before rationale's "BBB+=260, BBB=360, BBB-=610, BB+=940"), and the same after block gets the adjacent step right -- rationale A correctly says "The step from BBB- to BB+ alone is more than 300 factor points" (940 - 610 = 330). So this is one sentence the rewriter added on its own initiative, not content inherited from the source. Scope: key A is unaffected and the item is still answerable and single-keyed -- A ("default risk rises faster as ratings decline than ordinal spacing implies") remains the only true option against B ("all rating categories warrant identical treatment") and C ("credit risk does not differ across rating categories"). I am marking it fatal rather than style because the defect is a false quantitative claim shown to the learner after they commit, not prose that merely reads worse; the fix is to delete or correct the two ratios in rationale C.
fatal.quote_before: Risk varies dramatically.
fatal.quote_after: the likelihood of credit loss at BB+ (940) is more than twice that at BBB- (610) and roughly eight times that at A- (180)

fatal.detail: The reframe changed the question from "what does the sensitivity analysis show" to "which variable produces the largest reduction in IRR" — and under that new question A and C assert the SAME cause ("low traffic"), differing only in a number the stem never supplies. The stem gives the base case IRR (15%), the fixed-price contract, and the fact that low and high traffic cases were run; it gives no low-case IRR and no overrun IRR. So a learner can use the fixed-price-contract clue to eliminate B (cost risk is passed to the contractor), and is then left with two options that both answer the stem's question identically. Nothing in the item lets them prefer "10% to 11%" over "about 5%" — that discriminator exists only in the Year-0 dialogue the drill no longer reproduces, i.e. exactly the outside-the-item dependency rule 9 and the reframe ladder were meant to remove. In "before" the two options were at least distinguishable as whole statements of what the analysis showed, each carrying the base case plus its own case figure; the rewrite stripped A and C down to a shared stub plus an unsupported figure. The key is still factually right, but the item is no longer answerable from itself and C cannot be eliminated on reasoning. Fix is to put the low-case and overrun IRRs in the stem (ladder move 3) or to make the three options name three different causes (ladder move 2).

(1) Option C -- before 'No exit from ABC proved possible.', after 'No feasible exit from the stake.' -- was ruled out by the old stem's own words ('secondary sale ... successful'); the new stem asserts no outcome, so C is no longer excluded by anything in the item and the learner must recall how an unopenable case ended. Double-keyed. The stem stopped naming the method under test, which turned distractor C into a second correct answer. BEFORE the stem fixed the method ('Composite return using beginning assets plus weighted cash flows most likely:') and C was false because it offered beginning-of-period-only weighting AS that method: 'R_C = Sigma [r_pi x (V_0,pi / Sigma V_0,pi)], using only beginning-of-period values with no adjustment for external cash flows.' AFTER, the stem only establishes that cash flows occurred and asks an open question about GIPS ('Under the GIPS standards, each portfolio's return is most likely weighted by its:'), and C reads 'beginning-of-period assets alone.' Asset-weighting by beginning-of-period values is itself one of the three GIPS-permitted methods and is not voided by the presence of external cash flows - the sibling item r15_gips_los_e_q1 (index 1142) states exactly that in its own 'after' rationale A: 'Composite returns must be calculated by asset-weighting the individual portfolio returns using beginning-of-period values, by a method that reflects both beginning-of-period values and external cash flows, or by the Aggregate Return method.' So key A ('beginning assets plus day-weighted external cash flows') and distractor C are now both correct answers to the stem as written, and C's rationale still rebuts the old stem rather than the new one, arguing only that C 'is the beginning-assets method' and that 'The beginning assets plus weighted cash flows method instead uses V_pi = V_0 + Sigma(CF_i x w_i)' - a method the rewritten stem never asks about. Fix by restoring the method name to the stem (e.g. 'Under the beginning assets plus weighted cash flows method, ...'), which makes C false again for its original reason.

fatal.detail: Distractor A was unambiguously false before because it asserted exact identity on three separate dimensions: "Activist index and S&P 500 performance were identical across return, volatility, and Sharpe ratio." The rewrite deletes the dimensions and softens "identical" to "effectively identical.", and the stem simultaneously narrows the comparison to one dimension only ("the risk-adjusted performance ... relative to the S&P 500 Index"). The sole risk-adjusted datum is a Sharpe ratio of 0.56 against 0.54. Calling a 0.02 Sharpe gap "effectively identical" is a defensible reading of that evidence, especially since the source itself cautions that "it is difficult to conclude how much value activist investors add." A therefore now competes with the keyed B ("slightly better."), and the item is double-keyed: a learner who answers A cannot be shown to be wrong. The after-rationale for A concedes the problem and then defends A's falseness on grounds the new stem has excluded: "The risk-adjusted edge is slight, but return, volatility and Sharpe ratio all differ from the index's." Return and volatility are no longer what the stem asks about, so that defence does not reach the rewritten question. Fix by restoring a falsifiable A (e.g. "identical on return, volatility and Sharpe ratio.") or by widening the stem back to overall performance rather than risk-adjusted performance alone.

fatal.detail: The reframed stem invents a definition for the risk-decomposition percentages and gets it backwards. In "before" the figure is unlabeled beyond its exhibit name — option B reads "Manager A (factor diversified) 3.4% active risk, 0.76 Active Share, 3.6% avg sector deviation, Market source 98.0%", and the rationale lists it as "Source of risk Market 98.0%, Sectors -0.8%, Styles 1.8%, Unexplained 1.0%" (a decomposition summing to 100% and sitting beside both "Absolute risk 11.69%" and "Active risk 4.5%" for Manager C). The rewritten stem now declares that quantity to be "the share of active risk explained by the market factor", and the new rationale B repeats the new claim: factor-diversified managers "have nearly all of their active risk explained by the market factor". That is a share of TOTAL/ABSOLUTE risk in the source, not of active risk — the sibling item in this same reading and this same slice (r17_active_eq_pc_los_g_q3) states it explicitly in its own "after" rationale A: "market risk representing only 87.4% of total portfolio risk" and "more than 100% of its absolute risk attributed to the market factor". Substantively, a factor-diversified manager running 3.4% active risk at 0.76 Active Share does not get 98% of its TRACKING ERROR from market beta — market dominance at 98% is the signature of a total-risk decomposition. Consequence: under the stem as now written, the keyed option B ("Factor diversified: 3.4% active risk, 0.76 Active Share, 98.0% market factor") is not a true statement, and neither is any other option; B survives only as the least-wrong pairing. The key has not moved and the item is still answerable by elimination, so this is recoverable by deleting the word "active" from the stem and rationale B ("the share of total risk explained by the market factor"), but as committed the question asks about a quantity the data do not describe. Secondary, same stem: it promises a comparison on four dimensions including "average sector deviation", but the options carry only three — the sector-deviation figures (3.6%, 3.9%, 5.6%) that were in every "before" option were dropped.

fatal.detail: The rewrite moved the target allocation out of the options and into an unstated premise, so the item no longer contains the input it asks about. Before, the two competing options each asserted the target outright (A "target 40% stocks/60% bonds" vs C "a target allocation of 60% stocks and 40% bonds"), so the learner was matching a stated figure. After, the stem supplies only the current holdings and then refers to "that target" as if it had been given: "Grant's portfolio has risen from EUR 100 million to EUR 106 million over the last month and now holds EUR 46 million of European stocks and EUR 60 million of German bunds... Regarding that target and the rebalancing she needs...", with A "the target allocation is weighted more to bonds than to stocks" against C "the target allocation is weighted more to stocks than to bonds". Nothing in the stem determines which. The given data do not exclude C: a 60/40 target is arithmetically consistent with a EUR 106 million portfolio holding EUR 46M/EUR 60M (bonds EUR 40M -> EUR 60M, stocks EUR 60M -> EUR 46M), and that too would leave the weights "away from her target allocation". A is selectable only by recalling the curriculum example's parameters -- a reference the learner cannot open, which is the rule-9 failure the spec names -- or by judging it implausible that bunds rose 50% while stocks fell 23% in one month, i.e. by assuming bonds sat flat at EUR 60M and the whole EUR 6M gain was equity. The key does not move and A is still the only true option, but the question as rewritten is not answerable from itself. Fix: state the target in the stem (e.g. "against her target of 40% stocks and 60% bonds") and ask about the rebalancing instrument, or inline the pre-growth EUR 40M/EUR 60M split so the target is derivable.

fatal.detail: The qualifier that made distractor B false was deleted, leaving a claim that is defensible as true and so competing with the keyed answer. Before, B read "Always calculated on total return and never on return relative to a benchmark" — unambiguously false against the curriculum line "Performance can be calculated by using either total or relative return." After, B reads "based on total return rather than on return relative to a benchmark", which under the stem "Performance-based fees are most likely:" becomes a claim about the typical case rather than an absolute one. Read that way it is arguably correct, and the same reading supplies the support: performance fees are, per key option A itself, "common among hedge funds and less so among long-only strategies", and the reading states that "Private equity, hedge fund, and real estate partnerships commonly earn performance fees on total returns" (quoted in the sibling item r20_ims_los_i_q3 rationale C). So the vehicles that dominate the performance-fee universe commonly do charge on total return, and a strong candidate can defend B. The rationale confirms the mismatch: after-B still argues "Performance can be calculated by using either total return or return relative to a benchmark, so total return is not the only permitted basis" — a refutation of the "always/never" exclusivity the option no longer asserts. Restoring the absolute wording (e.g. "always based on total return and never on return relative to a benchmark") makes B false again and keeps A the single best answer.
fatal.quote_before: Always calculated on total return and never on return relative to a benchmark.
fatal.quote_after: based on total return rather than on return relative to a benchmark.

fatal.detail: The rewrite deleted the words that made distractor B false. fatal.detail: Distractor C lost its limiting qualifier, which was the whole of its falsity. Before: "Standard I(D) is limited to conduct resulting in criminal convictions for fraud" — false because of "is limited to". After: "Avoiding conduct that results in a criminal conviction for fraud", under the stem "Standard I(D) Misconduct most likely requires:". That residual claim is true — I(D) certainly requires avoiding fraud — so C is no longer a wrong statement, merely a narrower one than keyed B; compare sibling distractor A, which correctly kept its qualifier ("on the employer's premises during business hours only"). The rewritten C rationale confirms the mismatch, because it attacks a limitation the option no longer asserts: "No conviction, and no criminal charge, is required." The option as it now reads never says a conviction is required, so the rationale does not describe the option it is attached to.
fatal.quote_before: Standard I(D) is limited to conduct resulting in criminal convictions for fraud.
fatal.quote_after: Avoiding conduct that results in a criminal conviction for fraud.

fatal.detail: The rewrite made the party list a load-bearing half of the question and then dropped a party from the keyed option. The new stem explicitly asks two things: "The matters a member must avoid or disclose under Standard VI(A), AND THE PARTIES TO WHOM THAT DISCLOSURE RUNS, are most likely:". Standard VI(A) runs to "clients, prospective clients, and employer" — as the before-option C said verbatim. After the rewrite, keyed option C reads "to clients and employer", silently losing "prospective clients" on the one dimension the new stem puts in issue. Worse, distractor A now carries the complete and correct party list ("to clients, prospective clients, and employer") and is only wrong on the matter-trigger, so each of A and C is now half right on exactly one of the stem's two axes and the item no longer has a clean best answer. The after-rationale for C also contradicts the option it is explaining: it states the duty runs to "clients, prospective clients, and employer", a list the option itself no longer contains. The old stem ("Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts most likely requires:") did not interrogate the party list, so the omission was harmless there; the reframe is what makes it fatal. Fix is to restore "prospective clients" to option C.
fatal.quote_before: C: "Must AVOID or make full and fair disclosure of all matters that could reasonably be expected to impair their independence and objectivity and interfere with respective duties to their clients, prospective clients, and employer." | stem: "Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts most likely requires:"
fatal.quote_after: stem: "The matters a member must avoid or disclose under Standard VI(A), and the parties to whom that disclosure runs, are most likely:" | C: "Any matter that could reasonably be expected to impair objectivity, to clients and employer." | A: "Conflicts that have already impaired objectivity, to clients, prospective clients, and employer." | rationale C: "...interfere with their respective duties to clients, prospective clients, and employer..."

fatal.detail: The key's claim was narrowed from a general duty to one specific course of action, and the item's own rationale A then contradicts it as a 'must'. Before, C was the broad duty, which is satisfied whichever route Jorund takes. After, C requires her to take over coverage and produce a conclusion. But rationale A in 'after' states her options are to tell her supervisor she cannot cover the company OR to take over coverage and reach her own conclusions. Against a stem that now reads 'most likely must:', the rewritten C asserts as mandatory one of two alternatives the item itself presents as elective, so the key is only defensible by elimination against A (resign) and B (leave unchanged) rather than on its own terms. The source comment's operative line is weaker than the new option: she 'must issue only recommendations that reflect her independent and objective opinion' - which is vacuously met if she declines coverage.
fatal.quote_before: C: "Must be independent and objective."
fatal.quote_after: C: "reach and issue her own independent conclusion." / rationale A: "Her options are to tell her supervisor that she cannot cover the company under these constraints, or to take over coverage and reach her own independent conclusions."

fatal.quote_before: allocation short, so to avoid appearance of conflict Dill excludes his brother's account entirely
fatal.quote_after: an IPO suitable for many of his clients, including his brother, is undersubscribed. To avoid any appearance of a conflict of interest, Dill allocates no shares to his brother's account.
fatal.detail: The rewrite replaced the item's supply premise with its technical opposite. "allocation short" means the firm received fewer IPO shares than its suitable accounts could absorb — scarcity is precisely why an allocation decision had to be made and why a pro rata split is the test. "undersubscribed" means the opposite: demand fell short of supply, so shares were freely available and nothing had to be rationed. The key's own rationale in "after" still runs on the old, scarce-supply premise: "By not allocating the shares proportionately across all accounts for which he thought the IPO was suitable, Dill disadvantaged specific clients" — proportionate allocation is only an issue when supply is short, and distractor C in "after" ("would have violated Standard III(A) only by favoring his brother's account") is likewise built on the idea that giving the brother shares would come at other clients' expense, which it cannot under an undersubscribed offering. Rationale B in "after" compounds it by asserting the changed premise outright — "excluding it from a suitable but undersubscribed offering" — so the error is now stated in both the stem and a rationale. The key does not move (excluding a regular fee-paying client from a suitable investment is still a III(A) breach, so A remains the single best answer), but the stem as rewritten contradicts the reasoning the keyed rationale and distractor C depend on, which makes the item unteachable as written: a learner who reads "undersubscribed" correctly cannot reconstruct why proportionate allocation was ever at stake. Fix is one word — restore the short/insufficient allocation (e.g. "the firm's allocation is insufficient to fill all suitable accounts").

style.detail: Option A's assertion moved from a claim about the BASIS of universe design (index composition substituted for the firm's own process) to a claim about the universe's BREADTH (matching index breadth). The option is still false under the stem as rewritten -- the curriculum's criterion is the set of asset classes that receive a distinct allocation, kept otherwise as small as possible -- and rationale A in "after" still argues the original point ("Letting index composition set the universe ignores the firm's own investment process"), so the item is not broken and the key at C is unaffected. But the detail that carried the falsity explicitly ("without regard to firm-specific portfolio needs") is gone, leaving a distractor whose wrongness the learner must infer from the "as small as possible" guidance rather than read off the option. Worth noting as the one place in entries 0-9 where a distractor's claim is not the same claim said tersely. Not fatal: no collision with B ("as large as possible") or C, and A remains clearly wrong.
style.quote_before: Based on capitalization-weighted major indices without regard to firm-specific portfolio needs.
style.quote_after: as broad as the major capitalization-weighted indices.

style.detail: Distractor C gained a claim it did not previously make. Before, C asserted one direction (risk overestimated) plus a causal clause; the rewrite deleted the clause (correct under rule 1) but added a second, new assertion about expected return, turning C into the exact mirror of A. Not fatal: C is still false, still false for the same underlying reason, and rationale C in 'after' does cover both halves ('Both directions run the other way ... makes the sample overstate rather than understate ex ante expected return'). But per the per-letter same-claim requirement this is drift, not compression — the learner is now being asked to reject a proposition the item never put to them before.
style.quote_before: Overestimate ex ante risk because currency risk was still priced into asset yields.
style.quote_after: Overestimate ex ante risk and underestimate expected return.

style.detail: The key's own option lost the qualifier that located it. 'Cyclical' was the word that marked consumer confidence as a business-cycle phenomenon rather than a trend shock, and that is precisely the distinction the rewritten stem now turns on ('exogenous shocks to a country's trend rate of economic growth'). The 'after' rationale still reasons from the deleted word — 'A swing in consumer confidence is a business cycle phenomenon — a fluctuation around the trend' — so the rationale argues a qualifier the option no longer carries. Not fatal: consumer confidence appears on none of the six named shock categories (policy changes, new products and technologies, geopolitics, natural disasters, natural resources and critical inputs, financial crises) with or without 'cyclical', so A remains the unique correct answer and B and C remain on the list.
style.quote_before: A cyclical decline in consumer confidence.
style.quote_after: Weaker consumer confidence.

style.detail: Two linked residues. (1) Option A dropped 'then publishing the result', but rationale A still rests part of its argument on publishing — 'publishing on that basis passes the data-mining bias on to the reader' — so the rationale describes a clause the option no longer reads. (2) The compression moved A toward B: A is now 'Construct an economic explanation', B is 'Require an explicit economic rationale', and the only things separating them are A's 'once found' and B's out-of-sample test, where the 'before' pair were separated by the much blunter 'Inventing a plausible story ... after the fact'. Checked for collision and it does not collide: the stem asks for the 'most appropriate safeguard', and B alone carries the out-of-sample test, so B is still clearly best. Worth tightening A rather than fixing the key.
style.quote_before: Inventing a plausible story to explain the finding after the fact, then publishing the result.
style.quote_after: Construct an economic explanation for the relationship once found.

style.detail: The rewrite added explicit arithmetic to rationale A that does not match the figure option A actually carries. Option A is 4.0% (unchanged), but the new rationale works the subtraction out loud as 0.7% + 1.5% + 2.0% = 4.2%, hedged only by the word 'roughly'. The 'before' rationale made the same latent claim ('This value omits the dividend yield contribution') without exposing the 0.2pp gap, so nothing substantive changed; the rewrite just put a number on the page that contradicts the option it is explaining. Key C (6.0% = 0.7 + 1.5 + 2.0 + 1.8) is exact and still uniquely correct, so the item is not broken - the rationale simply now reads as if it describes an option that says 4.2%.
style.quote_before: A: "This value omits the dividend yield contribution."
style.quote_after: A: "This is roughly the nominal trend growth figure on its own — labor input growth plus labor productivity growth plus inflation, 0.7% + 1.5% + 2.0% = 4.2% — with the 1.8% dividend yield omitted." (option A reads "4.0%.")

style.detail: Reframed although the 'before' item was already self-contained, which the spec forbids ('Do not reframe an item that is already self-contained' — the old stem cited no exhibit and no curriculum text, so only rules 1-8 applied). The reframe is not wrong — key C is still the only correct direction and A/B are still false — but the correct option's second clause, which is the part of the LOS the item was testing, is now absent from the option set, leaving a bare sign question. The 'shorter-term yields rise more but with less price impact' nuance survives only in rationale C, i.e. after the learner has committed. A restatement under rules 1-8 would have shortened option C to something like 'Capital losses, concentrated in longer maturities.' and kept the tested distinction in play.
style.quote_before: stem: "Rising expected inflation that stays within the cyclical range would most likely affect nominal bonds by:" / C: "Generating capital losses as the expected-inflation component of yields rises; shorter-term yields rise more but with less price impact than longer yields."
style.quote_after: stem: "Rising expected inflation that stays within the expected cyclical range would most likely cause nominal bond prices to:" / A: "rise." B: "remain unchanged." C: "fall."

style.detail: Same pattern: reframed from a claim-selection item to a direction item although the 'before' stem was already self-contained, so the reframe ladder was not available to it. Substance is intact — key B 'rise.' is correct, A and C are still false, and rationale B keeps the idiosyncrasy caveat about lease length and the supply pipeline — but the reframe was triggered by option length (option C carried generator junk, 'That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay'), which a straight rewrite under rules 1-2 would have cured without changing what the item asks. Note also that rationale A still opens by rebutting a premise the option no longer states.
style.quote_before: stem: "Higher-than-expected inflation is most likely to affect real estate as follows:" / A: "Real estate is neutral because leases lock in nominal rates permanently." B: "Real estate benefits, coinciding with high demand, expectations of rental income rising faster than general inflation, and rising property values."
style.quote_after: stem: "Higher-than-expected inflation is most likely to cause property values and expected rental income to:" / A: "remain flat." B: "rise." C: "decline." / rationale A: "Leases do not lock in nominal rates permanently."

style.quote_before: No meaningful relationship with corporate excess returns.
style.quote_after: No meaningful change in excess returns on investment-grade corporate bonds.
style.detail: The distractor's claim shifts from 'no relationship' (a statement about correlation, which is what the item tests) to 'no meaningful change' (a statement about the level of excess returns). Its own rationale in 'after' still rebuts the old wording -- 'The relationship is meaningful and positive, with correlations of about 0.28 at a one-quarter horizon and 0.39 at a one-year horizon' -- so the rationale describes the option as it read before, not as it now reads. Not fatal: the option remains false either way and B is still the unambiguous best answer.

style.quote_before: Central banks explicitly coordinate real rate targeting internationally.
style.quote_after: Central banks coordinate real rate targets internationally.
style.detail: The qualifier 'explicitly' was dropped, and that qualifier is the hinge the rationale still turns on: 'Co-movement does not depend on explicit international coordination of real rate targets.' The option now makes the broader (and looser) claim that central banks coordinate real rate targets at all. Not fatal -- central banks do not target real rates, let alone coordinate such targets, so the option is still clearly wrong and the rationale's second clause ('not from any coordination agreement') still covers it -- but the distractor lost the word that made it crisply false.

All three rationales in 'after' refute or support their option by appeal to a specific market the rewritten stem no longer identifies, so they no longer describe the options as the learner now reads them. The key's rationale opens 'In the market at issue roughly half of the public equity market capitalization is represented by companies in the natural resources sector'; B is dismissed as 'not the concentration described in this market'; C is dismissed with 'The market contains substantial large companies'. With the Belvia setup gone from the stem, 'the market at issue' and 'this market' point at nothing the learner has seen, and the refutation of B reduces to an assertion about hidden facts rather than a reason. This is the same gap that makes the fatal finding above bite; even if B were reworded, the rationales would need to argue from the generic stem rather than from an unnamed market.
style.quote_before: rationale A: "Correct. The reading states roughly half of the public equity market is represented by natural resource companies..." / rationale B: "This is not the concentration described." / rationale C: "The reading does not describe this concentration."
style.quote_after: rationale A: "In the market at issue roughly half of the public equity market capitalization is represented by companies in the natural resources sector" / rationale B: "not the concentration described in this market" / rationale C: "The market contains substantial large companies, including the natural resource producers"

style.detail: Rationale B invents a substantive defence of the distractor that was not in 'before' and that sits awkwardly against the reading itself. The option is 'requires normality, and cannot handle time variation'; it is false because of the normality half, and 'before' said only that the pair is not the one identified. The rewrite instead tells the learner that a constant sample matrix 'handles time variation no worse than the alternatives it is being compared with'. That is defensible only within this question's comparison set (multi-factor and shrinkage matrices are also constant); read on its own it contradicts the reason the same reading goes on to introduce ARCH, namely that volatility is time-varying and a constant matrix cannot capture it. Not fatal: option B is still wrong, the key still sits on A, and the rationale does end with 'Neither item is one of the two problems identified.' Recommend trimming the clause to the non-identification point.
style.quote_before: Neither of these is the specific pair identified.
style.quote_after: a constant sample matrix handles time variation no worse than the alternatives it is being compared with

style.detail: The keyed option now refers to 'the two coefficients' but the stem no longer names or defines them. 'Before' at least pointed at the standard ARCH notation on the face of the options ('The parameter beta = 0', '(alpha + beta)'); the rewrite replaced those with 'A shock coefficient of zero' and 'A high sum of the two coefficients' while the stem was shortened to a single clause that introduces no model and no parameters, so the phrase has no antecedent in the item. A drill shows one question at a time, so the learner cannot pick the antecedent up from the neighbouring ARCH item (index 127), which does describe the specification. Not fatal, because within an ARCH model the two coefficients (on lagged variance and on the squared shock) are unambiguous and B is the only one of the three that could explain clustering at all. Fix is one clause in the stem, e.g. naming the coefficients on the lagged variance and the squared shock.
style.quote_before: According to the reading, the reason volatility 'clusters' at high or low levels in an ARCH model is most likely that: ... B. The higher the parameter (α + β), the more the variance 'remembers' what happened in the past.
style.quote_after: In an ARCH model, the clustering of volatility at high or low levels is most likely explained by: ... B. A high sum of the two coefficients.

style.detail: The rewritten C rationale still rebuts a clause that was deleted from option C. In "before", option C read "A rise in required return, so an overweight allocation is not warranted." — the overweight claim was part of the option. In "after", option C is only "A rise in the required return.", but its rationale closes by contrasting "attractive instead of unwarranted", which now answers a claim the learner never saw. The option itself is fine and the key is untouched; the rationale just no longer describes the option as it reads.
style.quote_before: C option: "A rise in required return, so an overweight allocation is not warranted."
style.quote_after: C option: "A rise in the required return." / C rationale: "the resulting price adjustment is what makes an overweight allocation attractive instead of unwarranted."

style.detail: Same pattern: option B's justifying clause was dropped but the rationale still argues against it. "before" option B was "Only the domestic-currency return, since currency movements will average out."; "after" is "The domestic-currency return alone." The option stays wrong (the word "alone" carries the falsity), so this is not fatal, but the rationale's opening rebuts an "averaging out" rationale that is no longer on the page.
style.quote_before: B option: "Only the domestic-currency return, since currency movements will average out."
style.quote_after: B option: "The domestic-currency return alone." / B rationale: "Currency exposure cannot be set aside on the view that movements average out."

style.detail: The key option lost the present-value framing that makes these items balance-sheet assets rather than income streams. Before, each element was explicitly a PV; after, two of the three are named as flows ("pension income", "expected inheritances"), which on an extended economic balance sheet are assets only as present values. The claim is not changed in substance and A remains unambiguously the best of the three (B and C are plainly conventional financial assets), and the rationale restores the PV wording in full ("the present value of expected pension income; and the present value of expected inheritances"), so this is imprecision rather than a broken question. Not fatal; noted because the stem asks what extended portfolio *assets* include.
style.quote_before: Human capital (PV of future earnings), PV of pension income, and PV of expected inheritances.
style.quote_after: human capital, pension income, and expected inheritances.

style.detail: The reframed stem drops the qualifier 'beyond volatility', which was what made the keyed option an exact answer and what set up the contrast with distractor C. The new stem asks for the full set of risk measures a mean-variance allocation can incorporate, but option B ('tracking risk and downside risk measures.') omits volatility itself -- which the item's own after-rationale for C concedes is incorporated ('Volatility is the baseline risk measure of the approach, not the only one it can accommodate.'). Not fatal: B carries no 'only' while A ('only tail risk measures...') and C ('volatility only.') are both exclusive and both false, so B is still unambiguously best and the key has not moved. Restoring 'beyond volatility' (or 'in addition to volatility') to the stem would make B exact again.
style.quote_before: A mean–variance asset allocation most likely can incorporate risk sensitivities beyond volatility, including:
style.quote_after: The risk measures that a mean-variance asset allocation can incorporate are most likely:

style.detail: Distractor C lost the universal qualifier "always". Before it read as an absolute claim that was false on its face; after, it is a general claim that is closer to defensible, since thin history genuinely is a problem for some narrow segments. Not fatal: the item is still single-keyed on B against the "most likely problematic because" stem, the exclusion in "before" did not rest on "always" either (its rationale said data availability is a secondary concern, not the primary reason), and the "after" rationale re-establishes the falsity by noting that many sub-asset classes do have long series available and that thin history is a secondary concern rather than the central objection. Flagged because qualifier deletion on a distractor is exactly the pattern this pass risks, and a reviewer should confirm the blanket claim is still read as false. Compare the sibling item r3_oaa_los_e_q7, where the same deletion (option C losing "only") was compensated by changing the stem verb from "include" to "comprises"; no such compensation was made here.
style.quote_before: Sub-asset classes always have insufficient historical data for optimization.
style.quote_after: sub-asset classes lack sufficient history for optimization.

style.detail: The keyed option lost the hedge that made it literally accurate. Before: 'Equity risk can be the dominant risk exposure even in a seemingly well-diversified portfolio.' After: 'Equity risk dominates a seemingly well-diversified portfolio.' The after-rationale still carries the hedged form — 'equity risk can be the dominant risk exposure even in a seemingly well-diversified portfolio' — so the option and its own rationale no longer say the same thing: the option asserts that equity risk does dominate such a portfolio, which is not a claim the reading makes. B remains clearly the best of the three (A is a separate implementation issue, C is explicitly denied) and the item is still answerable and correctly keyed, so this is not fatal, but 'can dominate' should be restored.
style.quote_before: Equity risk can be the dominant risk exposure even in a seemingly well-diversified portfolio.
style.quote_after: Equity risk dominates a seemingly well-diversified portfolio.

style.quote_before: W* = (μ − rf) × σ.
style.quote_after: Varies with excess return per unit of volatility, independent of risk aversion.
style.detail: The reframe reversed the direction of B's error in volatility. Before, B was wrong partly because it MULTIPLIED the risk premium by volatility: option "W* = (μ − rf) × σ." As rewritten, "per unit of volatility" states the opposite operation — the risk premium DIVIDED by σ (a Sharpe-ratio-like quantity). The option's own rationale was not updated to match and still asserts the old multiplication: "This formulation leaves risk aversion out altogether and mishandles variance, scaling by volatility instead, as in w* = (μ − rf) × σ." So the rationale describes a formula the option no longer states, violating the spec's requirement that a distractor's rationale "still has to describe it." Not keyed-breaking: B remains false on the surviving "independent of risk aversion" clause, and key C ("Falls with risk aversion and rises with excess return per unit of variance") is still the unambiguous best answer against A ("Rises with both risk aversion and variance"), whose rationale does match its option. Fix is to re-voice B as scaling with volatility (e.g. "Varies with excess return times volatility, independent of risk aversion") or to correct the rationale's formula.

The key's option now asserts something the stem has just removed from the problem. The stem reads "For an unconstrained mean-variance optimization, in which no budget constraint forces the weights to sum to 1" - so there is no budget constraint for the weights to breach, and option C has the mirror-image problem ("satisfy the budget constraint"). The after-rationale concedes the contradiction in as many words: "the solution does not respect a budget constraint that was never imposed." The substantive claim is unchanged and A is still uniquely correct (B is a frontier, not a point; C is the constrained outcome), so the item is not broken - but "that fail to sum to 100%" would carry the same claim without arguing against the stem. The dropped reverse-optimization qualifier is adequately covered by the stem's "most likely" and survives in the rationale.
style.quote_before: A single set of weights that is typically relatively extreme, with very large long and short positions, and which will not sum to 100% except in special reverse-optimization cases.
style.quote_after: Extreme long and short weights that breach the budget constraint.

style.detail: The expansion of distractor A's rationale added a clause whose sense is inverted. The before text was just "lambda = 0.5 corresponds to an aggressive investor with low risk aversion." The after text appends that such an investor "would accept a large variance penalty in exchange for expected return" - but the variance penalty in U = E(R) - 0.005(lambda)(sigma squared) is proportional to lambda, so at lambda = 0.5 the penalty the investor applies is small, not large. What the aggressive investor accepts is large variance, not a large penalty; as written it describes high risk aversion. Compare the correctly worded parallel clause in the after-rationale for C, "penalizing variance so heavily that the investor would hold a near-riskless allocation." The option itself (0.5) and the key (4) are unaffected, so this reads worse rather than breaking the item.
style.quote_before: λ = 0.5 corresponds to an aggressive investor with low risk aversion.
style.quote_after: A λ of 0.5 sits below the 1–10 range into which most investors' risk aversion falls and corresponds to an aggressive investor with low risk aversion, who would accept a large variance penalty in exchange for expected return.

style.detail: The rewritten stem stacks two CFA qualifiers on top of each other: "the most appropriate remedy is most likely:". The spec (rule 8) wants the stem to end with one qualifier, and the bank's own examples carry exactly one ("is closest to", "is most likely"). The original carried the qualifier once ("the reading recommends most likely"). Substance is unaffected -- key B ("Using the Black-Litterman model") is still the only approach that keeps the equilibrium anchor while admitting views, A and C both remain wrong for the reasons their rationales still give -- so this reads worse rather than breaking anything. Fix is to drop one: "the most appropriate remedy is to:" or "the recommended remedy is most likely:".
style.quote_before: For those with minor objections to using market-cap weights alone, the reading recommends most likely:
style.quote_after: the most appropriate remedy is most likely:

style.detail: The item was reframed off Exhibit 9 and the stem now reads generically ('A Monte Carlo projection of a retiree's wealth'), with no currency, no investor and no figures. The key's rationale still quotes the exhibit's CAF$ amounts, so a currency code that the self-contained stem never introduces appears from nowhere in the explanation. Not a defect in the question: option B is correct, A and C are false, every letter carries its prior claim, and the stem is answerable from itself. The fix would be to say 'a few hundred thousand' and 'ten times that' or to introduce the currency in the stem.
style.quote_before: The reading footnote explains that Exhibit 9's y-axis is a logarithmic scale — CAF$1 million is the same distance from CAF$100K as CAF$10 million is from CAF$1 million
style.quote_after: the spread of simulated terminal wealth from the 10th to the 90th percentile is very wide: the 10th percentile might be a few hundred thousand while the 90th exceeds CAF$10 million

style.detail: The rewrite made the keyed option the conspicuously longest of the three, where before the longest option was a distractor, so the "take the longest option" heuristic now names the key. After: A = 58 chars, B (key) = 88 chars, C = 64 chars. Before: A = 70, B = 122, C = 145, so length did not point at B. This is the length-asymmetry leak the spec calls a working answer key (drill_house_style.md lines 29-31, 41-42). Not fatal: each letter carries the same claim it carried before, B is still the only correct definition of minimum expectations, and both distractors remain false per their own rationales. B could carry the identical claim in distractor-length form, e.g. "The minimum return expected over the horizon at a given probability of success."
style.quote_before: B. "The minimum return expected to be earned over the given time horizon with a given minimum required probability of success." (122 chars) against distractor C. "The arithmetic mean of expected returns across the goal's investment horizon. The plain expected return carries no success-probability qualifier." (145 chars)
style.quote_after: B. "The minimum return expected over the horizon at a given required probability of success." (88 chars) against A. "The lowest return observed historically for the asset mix." (58) and C. "The arithmetic mean of expected returns over the goal's horizon." (64)

style.detail: Rationale A names a different second interpretation than the keyed option C does, so the two rationales disagree about what the pair is. Rationale A (after): 'The rebalancing story is instead the diversification return and the return to supplying liquidity - buying the asset class that has weakened and selling the one that has strengthened.' Rationale C (after) and option C instead give 'A diversification return and a short volatility return.' A learner who reads A first is told the second interpretation is liquidity supply, then told by C it is short volatility. IMPORTANT CAVEAT: this is NOT introduced by the rewrite - the identical sentence is already in before's rationale A ('Momentum and value are EQUITY factor premia; the rebalancing interpretations are the diversification return and being a supplier of liquidity (buying weakness, selling strength).'), and before's option A leaked the same text into the option itself. The rewrite only removed the leak from the option, which is an improvement. The key sits correctly in C, option C makes the same claim it made before, and A and B remain false. I report it only so the defect is on record; no rewrite action is implicated, and the item is otherwise sound.
style.quote_before: Incorrect. Momentum and value are EQUITY factor premia; the rebalancing interpretations are the diversification return and being a supplier of liquidity (buying weakness, selling strength).
style.quote_after: The rebalancing story is instead the diversification return and the return to supplying liquidity — buying the asset class that has weakened and selling the one that has strengthened.

style.detail: Distractor A lost the exclusivity qualifier that made it false. Before, A claimed regulatory position limits were THE MAIN disadvantage of growing AUM — an over-claim, false on its face regardless of whether position limits bite at all. After, the stem reads 'As assets under management grow, investment managers most likely incur disadvantages including:' and A is merely one item in a non-exclusive list, so the option now asserts only that narrower opportunity sets from regulatory position limits are AMONG the disadvantages of scale. That is defensible in substance (large managers do run into ownership/position limits that shrink the investable set), so the option is no longer cleanly false; its falsity now rests entirely on the curriculum's list of three being closed, which the item does not say. The key is not displaced — C still reproduces the curriculum's three disadvantages verbatim (larger trade sizes/price impact, style drift from inflows, slower decision making) and remains clearly the best of the three — so the item is not double-keyed, but the distractor is weaker than it was and the rationale ('not among the disadvantages of manager scale identified here') now has to appeal to an unstated closed list rather than to anything wrong in the option itself.
style.quote_before: The main AUM disadvantage is a narrower opportunity set imposed by regulatory position limits. That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay. Applied uniformly, it would bind at every horizon and every asset class.
style.quote_after: narrower opportunity sets imposed by regulatory position limits.

style.detail: Distractor A's attributed mechanism changed subject. style.detail: The rewrite added a fabricated, self-contradicting derivation to distractor A's rationale. It asserts the 25.0% answer "comes from applying the tax rate as a direct multiple rather than through the (1 - t) relationship" and then names that supposed error as "0.10 / 0.40". 0.40 is neither the tax rate (0.25) nor (1 - t) (0.75), so the denominator it attributes to the mistaken candidate has no relation to the tax rate at all, and the two halves of the sentence describe different errors. The arithmetic is incidentally true (0.10/0.40 = 0.25), and the rationale still tells the learner the correct conversion, so the item remains correctly keyed and answerable; the invented error path merely reads worse than the original one-liner it replaced. The real trap is simply mistaking the tax rate for the range.
style.quote_before: This is far too wide.
style.quote_after: This is far too wide. It comes from applying the tax rate as a direct multiple rather than through the (1 - t) relationship: the correct conversion is R_at = R_pt / (1 - t) = 0.10 / 0.75 = 13.3%, not 0.10 / 0.40 or any similar form that produces 25%. The equivalent range widens only modestly at a 25% tax rate.

style.detail: Option A no longer states a claim about trend signals; it names a thing that is not a candidate trend signal at all. Before, A asserted a proposition the learner could judge true or false ("Trend signals assume asset prices follow a random walk with no exploitable direction."). After, A is a noun phrase, "A random walk in prices over the trailing 12 months", offered as an answer to "A basic trend signal used in systematic TAA is most likely:" — a random walk is a price process, not a signal, so the option is a category error rather than a wrong signal. It also breaks the parallelism of rule 7: B and C are both return measures ("The most recent 12-month return." / "The average return over the past 30 years.") while A is a process description, which makes A visibly the odd one out and narrows the real choice to B versus C. Not fatal: A is still unambiguously not the answer, the key B is still correct and clearly best, and rationale A still explains the same reason it is wrong ("If asset prices followed a random walk, past returns would carry no information about future returns and trend following would be pointless."). The repair is to keep A a signal, e.g. "A randomly selected direction for the next 12 months."
style.quote_before: Trend signals assume asset prices follow a random walk with no exploitable direction.
style.quote_after: A random walk in prices over the trailing 12 months.

style.quote_after: The goals of ESG integration are to reduce financial risks and enhance financial returns by identifying and valuing risks or opportunities that are not typically identified and valued.

style.detail: Distractor B gained a clause it did not carry before. Before, B asserted only the inverse convexity-duration relationship; after, it leads with the TRUE proposition that duration rises linearly with maturity and only its second clause is false. The option is still wrong (a conjunction with one false clause), it is still wrong for the same reason, and rationale B still describes it correctly ('The relationship is direct, not inverse'), so the item is NOT broken and the key at A is still uniquely best. style.detail: Key A and distractor B now differ only by the words "compounded" and "multiplied", and under one natural reading they say the same thing. Before, B carried its own arithmetic and was unambiguously false: it asserted the bare product of the two NET returns, R_DC = R_FC x R_FX, which is visibly not (1 + R_FC)(1 + R_FX) - 1. The rewrite stripped that formula, leaving "the foreign-currency and currency returns multiplied" -- but compounding IS the multiplication of the two GROSS returns, so a learner who reads B as "multiply the returns (as 1 + R factors)" sees a second correct option. A is still the better answer, because "compounded" is the curriculum's own word for the relationship and the stem asks for the most likely, so this is not mis-keyed or double-keyed; but the distractor lost the detail that made it cleanly wrong, and the option set no longer stands on its own -- only B's rationale ("The bare product R_FC x R_FX is only the cross-term of that expansion") restores the distinction, and the learner reads that after committing. The fix is to keep the distinction visible in the option itself, e.g. "The foreign-currency and currency returns multiplied together as a cross-product."
style.quote_before: The domestic-currency return on a foreign bond is the product of the two returns: R_DC = R_FC × R_FX.
style.quote_after: The foreign-currency and currency returns multiplied.

style.detail: The keyed option's content was broadened rather than restated tersely: before, B named two liability-based approaches (cash flow matching and duration matching, each with its definition in parentheses); after, it names three (cash flow matching, duration matching, and contingent immunization). This is a genuine change to what letter B asserts, not a shortening of the same assertion. It is not fatal: the stem asks what liability-based mandates 'most likely include', the before-rationale for B already enumerated all three approaches as the liability-based family, so the new B is still true, still the best of the three, and the key has not moved. style.detail: The key's proposition was replaced with its consequence, and the old proposition was moved into the stem. Before, C asserted the shared data dependence itself: "Both rely on reported returns of alternatives, which are subject to STALE PRICING and APPRAISAL SMOOTHING." After, C asserts the resulting bias: "Understated volatility in both, biasing toward overallocation." The stem now supplies the old C as a given — before: "Weakness common to BOTH the asset-class and risk-factor approaches when applied to alternatives most likely:" / after: "Smoothed and stale reported returns on alternative investments affect the asset-class approach and the risk-factor approach to allocation most likely as:" So the tested content shifts from recognizing that both approaches inherit the smoothed-returns problem to knowing the direction of the bias. NOT fatal: the new C is correct (it is stated verbatim in the before rationale, "both approaches understate true volatility and correlations, biasing efficient frontiers toward overallocation to alternatives"), A and B remain false (A reverses direction, B is refuted because factor decomposition is estimated from the same return series), the key stays in C and the item is unambiguous and answerable. Flagged only because the item was already self-contained (no exhibit, no citation), and the spec says "Do not reframe an item that is already self-contained"; the shortening could have been done as a restatement of the original claim instead. Secondary: option B, "Distortion of the asset-class approach only.", is not grammatically parallel with A and C, which are both "<direction> volatility in both, biasing toward <direction>".

These are not the same claim: the original admitted a parallel shift (yields move, slope does not), the rewrite admits only a frozen curve. style.detail: The rewrite de-Unicoded the key rate duration formula in rationale B and in doing so changed the operator from a discrete change to a derivative. 'Before' carries the curriculum's Equation 10 as KeyRateDur_k = -(1/PV) x (DeltaPV / Delta r_k) with the proper minus sign, multiplication sign and Sigma for the summation; 'after' writes dPV / dr_k with an ASCII hyphen, a lowercase letter x for the multiplication sign, and spells the summation out as 'sum of KeyRateDur_k = EffDur'. Delta -> d promotes a finite-difference definition into a partial derivative, which is not what the reading states, and the item's sibling r8_ycs_los_d_q5 kept Delta, the multiplication sign and the true minus sign in its EffDur / EffCon equations, so the two rewritten rationales now render the same notation two different ways. No option or key is affected and the reasoning around the formula is intact and in fact expanded (the rewrite correctly adds 'while the other key rates are held constant'), so this reads worse rather than breaking the question.

style.detail: Dropping the equation from distractor B removed the only thing that made it unambiguously false. Before, B read 'the product of the two component returns: R_DC = R_FC x R_FX' — the formula pinned it to net returns. After, B is 'the product of the foreign-currency return and the FX return', and the key A is 'the compounded combination of the foreign-currency return and the FX return'. The correct relationship IS a product (of gross returns), so B is now only wrong if the learner reads 'product' as strictly the product of net returns and 'compounded' as the gross-return product minus one. A is still the better option and the key does not move, so this is not fatal, but the gap between A and B now rests on an unstated gross-versus-net reading rather than on anything in the option text. The after rationale B still argues against net returns ('Multiplying the two net returns together, R_FC x R_FX, is not the compounding relationship'), which is a claim the option as it now reads does not quite make.
style.quote_before: The domestic-currency return on a foreign bond is the product of the two component returns: R_DC = R_FC × R_FX.
style.quote_after: the product of the foreign-currency return and the FX return.

style.detail: The key's slot lost both the spot rate and the compounding. Before, B carried the full relation 'F(DC/FC, T) = S_0(DC/FC) x [(1 + r_DC)^T / (1 + r_FC)^T]'. After, it reads 'a forward rate scaled by the ratio of the two risk-free rates' — which omits the spot rate that is actually being scaled (A and C both still reference spot, so B is now the only option that does not), and says 'the ratio of the two risk-free rates' where CIP uses the ratio of the gross rates compounded over T, (1 + r_DC)^T / (1 + r_FC)^T. The after rationale B still states the precise form, so the rationale is now more specific than the option it explains. B remains uniquely defensible against 'no link between the forward and spot exchange rates' and 'a forward rate equal to the spot rate in all circumstances', so the key is safe; the claim is just looser than it was.
