The item's own rationale for A fixes the intended sense ("the shorter-dated option has the larger, more negative theta"), and curriculum usage treats greater/larger theta as magnitude, so the key is still the best answer and I do not call this fatal. But the before text could not be misread this way and the after text can, in an item whose whole subject is the comparison of two negative numbers. Saying "larger in magnitude" or "decays faster" would remove the second reading.

Rationale A gained a clause the original did not have, and it is not strictly true. The original rested option A's wrongness entirely on the geometry of the structure: a single shared strike collapses the floor-and-cap band, so the position is not a collar. The rewrite keeps that and then appends that there is no reason the two premiums would be equal at a common strike. By put-call parity a put and a call struck at the forward price carry identical premiums, and at an at-the-money common strike they are near enough equal in practice, so premium equality at a common strike is exactly the case a learner is likely to have met. Not fatal: option A is still a wrong description of a zero-cost collar for the original reason, the key stays at B ('buying a put and writing a call with the same premium'), and distractor C ('buying a put and buying a call whose premiums offset') stays false as a straddle costing two premiums. Only the appended teaching point is unsound.
style.quote_before: Zero cost comes from matching PREMIUMS, not strikes; equal strikes would collapse the protective range to a single price.
style.quote_after: If the put and the call shared one exercise price, the protective range would collapse to that single price, fixing the payoff rather than leaving a band between a floor and a cap, and there is no reason the two premiums would be equal at a common strike in any case.

style.detail: Option C lost the timing qualifier that carried its falsity, and its rationale still argues the dropped qualifier. Before, C was false because the move was said to come 'before expiration' — i.e. before the written near-term leg expires, which is exactly what destroys the position. As rewritten, C is the untimed claim 'profit from a large directional move', and a long calendar spread trader does hold a directional view that is meant to pay off eventually (the sibling item r16_opt_los_g_q3 keys precisely that: 'a directional view, with the price move not expected to be imminent'). The key is not in danger — the curriculum states time decay is the primary motivation, so B remains clearly best and the item is not double-keyed — but C is no longer wrong for the reason its rationale gives: the 'after' rationale reads 'An imminent large move is the outcome that damages the written near-term leg, which the trader needs to expire worthless', and 'imminent' is a word the option no longer contains. Restoring the qualifier (e.g. 'profit from a large directional move before the near-term expiration.') costs nothing and is still well inside the length target.
style.quote_before: Profiting from a large DIRECTIONAL MOVE in the underlying before expiration. That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay.
style.quote_after: profit from a large directional move.

style.detail: The rewrite narrowed option C to the implied-volatility clause alone, but the after-rationale for C still rebuts the dropped 'stable market' clause, so it describes the option as it used to read rather than as it now reads. Before, option C was 'A stable market or a DECREASE in implied volatility will help a LONG calendar spread.' After, it is only 'long, when implied volatility falls.' The after-rationale, however, spends its middle on a condition the option no longer contains: 'A stable market does favor the long calendar spread, since the near-dated option it has sold decays faster than the distant option it holds, but pairing that stable market with a decline in implied volatility reverses the vega effect and works against the position.' Not fatal: C is still wrong for the same reason (a long calendar spread is net long the higher-vega distant option, so falling implied volatility hurts it), and the first sentence of the rationale says exactly that. The 'pairing that stable market with' clause simply has nothing left to attach to.
style.quote_before: A stable market or a DECREASE in implied volatility will help a LONG calendar spread.
style.quote_after: A stable market does favor the long calendar spread, since the near-dated option it has sold decays faster than the distant option it holds, but pairing that stable market with a decline in implied volatility reverses the vega effect and works against the position.

style.detail: The rewrite added a causal gloss to distractor B's rationale that is economically incorrect. The 58-strike call costs GBP 1.00 more than the 60-strike call (GBP 4.00 vs GBP 3.00) but pays GBP 2.00 more at the GBP 70 target (payoff 12 vs 10; profit GBP 8.00 vs GBP 7.00), so the extra premium buys MORE total profit, not value the client 'would have captured anyway'. The genuine reason the 58-strike loses the comparison is the per-unit-of-premium ratio, (70-62)/4.00 = 2.0 against (70-63)/3.00 = 2.3, which the same rationale already states correctly from the curriculum. The key is unaffected and the item is not broken, so this is a readability/accuracy nit in explanatory text the rewrite invented rather than preserved.
style.quote_before: B: "Higher delta ≠ better $ profit per premium."
style.quote_after: because the extra £1.00 of premium buys intrinsic value the client would have captured anyway.

style.detail: The reframe inlines the betas correctly (every figure matches the "before" rationale: 0.99/-0.16/0.02/-0.01, 0.92/-0.23/0.41/0.13, 0.90/0.13/0.59/0.09, alphas 0.05%/-0.05%/-0.35%) and the key still sits in B, so the item is answerable and not mis-keyed. But the new stem labels the two indexes by capitalization, which telegraphs half of each option's cap-tilt claim: the stem already calls the first series "a broad large-cap index" and the second "a large-cap value index", so B's "a large-cap tilt" is pre-confirmed and C's "a small-cap tilt" is pre-refuted without the learner ever interpreting the -0.16 and -0.23 size betas, which is the judgment the item is testing. The old stem ("The Exhibit 2 factor exposures...") named the series as Russell 1000 / Russell 1000 Value and carried no cap label. Labeling them neutrally (a broad index, a value index) would restore the test.
style.quote_before: The Exhibit 2 factor exposures over 26-year period most likely show:
style.quote_after: 0.92, −0.23, 0.41 and 0.13 for a large-cap value index ... C: "a small-cap tilt and negligible value exposure for the value index."

style.detail: The reframe is substantively clean: IC 0.10, TC 0.25, active risk 6% and BR = 1 are all supplied in the stem, 0.10 x 1 x 6% x 0.25 = 0.15% = 15 bps, the key stays in C, and both distractors are false (0 bps, and 60 bps as the TC-omitted trap). The style defect is option order: the three candidate values now run 0, 60, 15 rather than ascending, which the bank's numeric items never do ("A. 1.5% B. 2.0% C. 2.8%"). Ascending order would move the key to B, so this is a forced consequence of the key-in-slot constraint rather than a fixable slip, but it reads as a scrambled value list.
style.quote_before: C: "Manager could expect to generate active return of 15 bps yearly on average with single independent decision (0.10 × √1 × 6% × 0.25 = 0.15%)."
style.quote_after: A: "0 bps." B: "60 bps." C: "15 bps."

style.detail: The claim survives (sector counting is still the wrong basis for breadth, and the "after" rationale still describes it as such: "Independence is defined by the correlation between decisions, not by the label on a bucket"), so this is not fatal. But the shortening garbles the agent: sectors do not hold active positions, the manager takes active positions in sectors. The parallel shape of the other two options ("the number of securities held", "the number of uncorrelated active decisions") would be kept by "the number of sectors with active positions".
style.quote_before: The number of sectors in which the manager takes active positions.
style.quote_after: the number of sectors holding active positions.

style.detail: Key A ("maximize a risk-adjusted return.") is still uniquely correct, so the item is not mis-keyed or unanswerable — but the two distractors have merged into one claim. In "before", B was a claim about practice and C was a claim about the source text, which kept them distinct: B "Portfolio construction proceeds without any objective function." versus C "The reading specifies no framework for construction objectives." Dropping the citation from C (correct under rule 9) re-voiced it as a claim about practice: "follow no specified objective framework." Read against the new stem "Equity portfolio construction, as commonly practiced, is most likely to:", B and C now assert the same thing — no objective function / no specified objective framework — so letter C no longer carries the claim it carried before and the item effectively offers two options instead of three. Both are false, so severity is style, not fatal. A fix would be to restore a distinguishing qualifier to C (e.g. a different wrong objective, such as maximizing absolute return without regard to risk) rather than a second phrasing of B.
style.quote_before: The reading specifies no framework for construction objectives.
style.quote_after: follow no specified objective framework.

style.detail: The rewrite correctly stripped the uncitable source, but the replacement stem still leans on it implicitly: it asks which fund is paired with "its reported" active risk and Active Share without ever saying who reported them or supplying the figures. The item stays answerable, because the keyed option B ("Vanguard Index Fund, 0.0% active risk and 0.00 Active Share.") is true by the definition of an index fund, and the Exhibit 8 table survives in full inside rationale B. But distractors A ("AIM Constellation, 5.4% active risk and 0.93 Active Share.") and C ("T. Rowe Price Mid-Cap Value, 9.7% active risk and 0.66 Active Share.") are figure swaps the learner has no in-item basis to reject, so the item is carried entirely by B being self-evident rather than by the discrimination it was written to test. Not fatal; it reads as a dangling reference. Naming the orientation in the stem (e.g. an indexed fund versus two active funds) or inlining the comparison would close it.
style.quote_before: Petajisto (2013) Exhibit 8 examples — Vanguard Index Fund, RiverSource Disciplined Equity, T. Rowe Price Mid-Cap Value, AIM Constellation most likely:
style.quote_after: The fund most likely paired correctly with its reported active risk and Active Share is:

style.detail: The rewrite narrowed the stem's subject from the whole three-row attribution to the fund's row alone, which leaves distractor B as a non-sequitur rather than a coherent candidate answer. Before, the stem was about the attribution as a whole ('The Exhibit 12 absolute risk factor attribution for Russell 1000, Russell 1000 Value, Value Fund most likely:') and B was a sensible claim about that table omitting the index rows. After, the stem asks what 'the fund's attribution most likely shows', so B reads as 'the fund's attribution shows no comparable attribution for the indexes' - the fund's own attribution is not the kind of thing that could show or not show a row for the indexes. B is still unambiguously wrong and the key (C, the larger unexplained share, 25.9% against 0.7% and 5.4%) is still uniquely correct, so the item is answerable and correctly keyed; the option is merely no longer parallel with A and C as a thing the fund's attribution could show. Not fatal.
style.quote_before: stem: "The Exhibit 12 absolute risk factor attribution for Russell 1000, Russell 1000 Value, Value Fund most likely:" / B: "The exhibit attributes risk for the funds but omits the benchmark indexes."
style.quote_after: stem: "In an absolute risk factor attribution of a broad market index, a value index, and an actively managed value fund, the fund's attribution most likely shows:" / B: "no comparable attribution for the indexes."

style.detail: Distractors A and C state the same claim, so the item effectively offers two choices rather than three. After: A is "constant throughout the period." and C is "unvarying from year to year." — there is no state of the world in which one is true and the other false, and the two rationales argue identically (A: "Volatility is time varying, not constant"; C: "The variation is the central feature of the record"). This is NOT introduced by the rewrite: before, A read "Exhibit 20 shows S&P 500 volatility constant across 1995-2020." and C read "The exhibit shows no variation in realized volatility over the period.", which collide in the same way. The key (B) is unaffected and the item is still answerable and correctly keyed, so this is style only; flagging it because the rewrite was the last chance to differentiate one of the two.
style.quote_before: A: "Exhibit 20 shows S&P 500 volatility constant across 1995–2020." / C: "The exhibit shows no variation in realized volatility over the period."
style.quote_after: A: "constant throughout the period." / C: "unvarying from year to year."

style.detail: Rationale A argues against two figures that the rewrite removed from the item, so the learner has nothing to match them to. In "before", option A carried five figures — "MSCI World: 7.0% return, 20.0% volatility, 500 securities, 15% turnover, 1.5% dividend yield" — and the rationale's reply covered all of them. In "after", option A was trimmed to three figures ("7.0% return, 20.0% volatility, 500 securities.") because turnover and yield moved into the stem for the benchmark, but rationale A still rebuts "a 500-stock, 15% turnover, 1.5% yield portfolio". The 15% and 1.5% now appear nowhere else in the stem, the options or the other rationales — they are orphaned. Not fatal: the key (C) is still the only coherent benchmark profile, since B's figures are assigned to the portfolio by the stem itself and A's 20.0% volatility and 500 securities are implausible for a broad developed-market index. The rationale merely describes an option that no longer reads that way.
style.quote_before: "A": "MSCI World: 7.0% return, 20.0% volatility, 500 securities, 15% turnover, 1.5% dividend yield."
style.quote_after: "A": "7.0% return, 20.0% volatility, 500 securities." / rationale A: "rather than with a 500-stock, 15% turnover, 1.5% yield portfolio"

style.detail: The rewritten stem relabels the factor-attribution percentages as a decomposition of ACTIVE risk; in "before" they are a decomposition of the portfolio's risk generally (Market 69.2% + Sectors 11.6% + Styles 9.7% + Unexplained 9.5% = 100%, reported alongside absolute risk of 11.69% and active risk of only 4.5%). A manager with 0.87 Active Share would not have 69.2% of ACTIVE risk explained by the market factor; that figure belongs to the total/absolute risk attribution. The same relabeling is carried into rationale B in "after" ("only 69.2% of active risk is explained by the market factor, with 11.6% from sectors, 9.7% from styles, and 9.5% unexplained"), while rationale C in "after" correctly keeps the neutral wording ("The sources of risk show significantly less exposure to the market factor at 69.2%"). Not fatal: key C ("the cash holding dampens portfolio volatility") is still the only correct option, since the stem supplies beta 1.28 against absolute risk of 11.69% only slightly above the index's, which makes A false and C true. The defect is a factual mislabel in the stem, not a broken key.
style.quote_before: Twenty-one holdings, 0.87 Active Share, high sector deviation, and 9.5% unexplained risk indicate a benchmark-agnostic, concentrated strategy — the opposite of a closet indexer, and Market explains only 69.2% of risk.
style.quote_after: an average sector deviation of 5.6%, and 69.2% of active risk explained by the market factor. The most likely interpretation of this profile is that:

style.detail: The rewrite converted the formula options to prose but stacked two division words in one phrase, so the key's arithmetic is ambiguous on a first read. 'divided by cheapest-to-deliver BPV over the conversion factor' is intended as (BPV_T - BPV_P) / (BPV_CTD/CF), i.e. the correct general form [(BPV_T - BPV_P)/BPV_CTD] x CF that the rationale states. A reader who attaches 'over the conversion factor' to the whole quotient instead gets (BPV_T - BPV_P)/BPV_CTD/CF, which is wrong, and under that parse no option is correct: A has the numerator reversed and B multiplies by CF. The same phrase appears in A, so the ambiguity does not move the key, and the natural reading of 'BPV_CTD over the conversion factor' as a single noun phrase is the intended one - hence style, not fatal. Not a defect in meaning: before and after carry the same three claims.
style.quote_before: BPV_HR = [(BPV_T - BPV_P) / BPV_F] where BPV_F ≈ BPV_CTD / CF.
style.quote_after: target BPV less portfolio BPV, divided by cheapest-to-deliver BPV over the conversion factor.

style.detail: House style rule 7 requires the three options to be the same kind of thing - 'Either all three options carry figures or none of them do.' Here A is an action ('the manager buys 36 Euro-Bund futures contracts') while B and C are two euro basis point values. The mixed shape survived the rewrite rather than being introduced by it (before, A was likewise an action and B/C were formulas), and because two of the three carry figures the odd-one-out heuristic does not name the key, so this is cosmetic. Worth noting only because the rewrite was the pass that was supposed to make the three options parallel and did not. The item itself is sound: B = 9.50 x 0.0001 x €49,531,000 = €47,054.45 is verifiable from the stem, C is the target BPV and false, and A is ruled out on direction alone (lowering duration requires selling).
style.quote_before: Buy 36 Euro-Bund futures contracts.
style.quote_after: the manager buys 36 Euro-Bund futures contracts.

style.detail: Recasting the options as lowercase continuations of the new stem left A reading ungrammatically against it: the stem is 'A prime broker's collateral requirement for a short position is most likely to:', so A reads 'a collateral requirement ... is most likely to count all asset types at full market value.' A requirement does not count assets; the collateral calculation does. In 'before' this was a standalone sentence with the right subject. The claim is unchanged and still false per its own rationale (a T-bill counts at 100%, a high-yield bond only partially), so nothing is broken. Related and also cosmetic: A and B describe properties of the requirement while the key C describes its purpose, which leaves the key the only purpose-clause among the three - an asymmetry that was present before the rewrite too.
style.quote_before: All asset types count at 100% of market value toward the collateral requirement.
style.quote_after: count all asset types at full market value.

style.detail: The rewrite replaced a short, correct distractor rationale with a longer one whose added explanatory clause reasons backwards. Before, rationale A said only that the basis subtracts: 'Incorrect. The basis is NEGATIVE - it subtracts: 1.95% - 15 bps = 1.80%.' After, it asserts that adding the basis 'would turn a funding saving into a funding cost, which is the opposite of what a negative quoted basis does.' The firm RECEIVES the Canadian dollar leg, so raising that rate helps it. Working the item's own numbers: at -15 bps the firm receives CAD50M x 1.80% x 180/360 = CAD450,000 and its total six-month cost is USD660,000 (the figure rationale C still quotes); at +15 bps it would receive CAD525,000 and pay USD600,000, against USD700,000 for the straight US dollar loan. Adding the basis therefore enlarges the funding saving rather than turning it into a cost, and the negative basis is what shrinks it. The stem, the three option values and the keyed rationale C are all unaffected, so the item is still correctly keyed and answerable - only this distractor rationale now teaches a reversed intuition about which direction the basis cuts.
style.quote_before: Incorrect. The basis is NEGATIVE — it subtracts: 1.95% − 15 bps = 1.80%.
style.quote_after: Adding the basis would raise the rate the firm receives on the Canadian dollar leg and would turn a funding saving into a funding cost, which is the opposite of what a negative quoted basis does.

style.detail: The key's option was compressed from the explicit formula to the phrase "the beta gap", a term the stem never defines and which loses the direction of the subtraction. The correct hedge ratio depends on the signed quantity (beta_T - beta_S) -- that sign is what tells the manager to buy rather than sell -- and "gap" is direction-agnostic. The key is still unambiguously the best of the three (B multiplies the betas, C sums them and inverts S/F), so this is not fatal, but the rewritten option is less precise than the claim it replaced and the defining phrase now appears only in the rationale the learner reads after committing.
style.quote_before: N_f = [(β_T - β_S) / β_f] × (S/F) where β_T is target beta, β_S is portfolio beta, β_f is beta of futures, S is market value of stock portfolio, F is value per futures contract.
style.quote_after: the beta gap divided by the futures beta, times the portfolio-to-contract value ratio.

style.detail: The rewritten key rationale rounds the mark-to-market to -$112,962.93, but the formula printed in that same rationale yields -$112,962.963: 1,250 x 0.987654 x [(6/12)(256) + (6/12)(361) - 400] = -112,962.96. The rewrite faithfully rounded the figure carried in "before" (-$112,962.9263), which was itself a digit-transposition, so the rewrite did not originate the error -- but a learner who works the arithmetic from the formula now in front of them gets a value three cents off the one stated beside it. The stem as reframed asks only for the variance notional (1,250), and the final $112,963 is unaffected, so nothing about the key or the distractors is in doubt.

The rewritten stem asserts the existence of the very instruments distractor B denies, so B is refuted by the stem rather than by knowledge of the LOS. Before, the stem was contentless ("VIX options most likely:") and B's claim that VIX options were never introduced had to be judged on its merits; after, the stem opens "The volatility exposure provided by exchange-listed VIX options...", which presupposes they are exchange-listed and trading, while B still reads "nonexistent, because no VIX options have been introduced." The key (C) remains uniquely correct and B remains false, so the item is not broken, but one of the three options is now eliminable without reading past the stem. Dropping "exchange-listed" from the stem would restore the discrimination.
style.quote_before: VIX options most likely:
style.quote_after: The volatility exposure provided by exchange-listed VIX options is most likely:

style.detail: Rationale B gained an illustrative figure that has no antecedent anywhere in the reframed item. The item is now a generic conceptual question about overlays -- the stem is "A manager uses futures and swaps to change a portfolio's equity and interest rate exposures over a short horizon instead of trading the underlying securities" -- and carries no portfolio, no contract count and no beta. The rounding example is borrowed from the Grant item (r17_swf_los_e_q7, where Nf = -123.57 rounds to 124 contracts), so a learner reading this item alone meets "123.57" cold. The 'before' rationale made the same point generically, with no numbers, and read correctly on its own. Not fatal: the key (C) and both distractors are unaffected, and the sentence's actual argument -- that contract rounding, beta/duration drift, CTD and conversion-factor changes and roll costs leave basis risk -- survives without the figure.
style.quote_before: Incorrect. Futures- and swap-based overlays still carry basis and tracking risk versus the underlying exposure (contract rounding, beta estimates, roll costs); their advantage is speed, lower cost, and leaving holdings undisturbed — not eliminating tracking risk.
style.quote_after: Contracts trade in whole units, so the notional rounds — 123.57 contracts becomes 124 — betas and modified durations are estimates that drift

style.detail: The rewrite ADDED a directional gloss to the key's rationale that states the exchange rate move backwards. The after stem supplies 'the CAD/EUR exchange rate moves from 1.4500 to 1.4700'; in CFA P/B notation CAD/EUR is CAD per EUR, so the EUR buys MORE CAD after the move (1.45 -> 1.47) and it is the CAD that buys fewer EUR (0.6897 -> 0.6803) -- which is exactly why R_FX = -1.364% for a eurozone investor. The before rationale carried no such gloss; it ended on the arithmetic. The sibling item r18_currfx_los_a_q6 reads the identical quote correctly in its own after rationale C ('The EUR appreciated against the CAD'), so the two rewritten items now contradict each other on the same data. This is not cosmetic: the inversion trap is the item -- distractor C is precisely 'failing to invert the CAD/EUR quote for the eurozone investor' -- and the key's own rationale now narrates the move in the direction the distractor takes, reinforcing the error the question exists to test. Key, options and arithmetic are all still correct and the item remains answerable and correctly keyed, so it is not fatal by the stated definition, but the defect is factual and should not be filed as a readability nit.
style.quote_after: Both components are negative here — the asset fell in CAD terms and the EUR bought fewer CAD after the move — so the losses compound.

style.detail: The rewrite dropped the IPS scoping from the stem. Before, the stem restricted the question to IPS inputs, which is what made option A (forward points) out of scope by construction. The after-stem asks only what the program design depends on, and elsewhere in this same LOS set (r18_currfx_los_c_q7) the curriculum is cited as saying market conditions, specifically 'movements in forward points (expected roll yield)', affect the hedging decision and that 'when forward points move against hedger, amount of hedging activity typically declines'. So A is now weakly defensible rather than plainly out of scope. Keyed B ('The general objectives of the portfolio.') is still the clearly best of the three under 'most likely', and the B rationale still grounds it in the IPS, so this is not fatal — but the stem no longer carries the qualifier that excluded A, and the exclusion now rests only on the rationale the learner reads afterwards.
style.quote_before: IPS variables affecting currency management program design most likely:
style.quote_after: The design of a portfolio's currency management program is most likely to depend on:

style.detail: The keyed option lost the curriculum's hedge. Before it read as a conditional observation about what technicians sometimes read into a crossover; after it asserts flatly that a crossover 'marks' a break-out point. The claim is still correct enough to be the best of the three and the key does not move, so this is not fatal, but the rewrite states as a rule what the reading states as a convention, and the option also drops the concrete '50-day' / '200-day' naming in favour of generic 'short- and long-term' (the rationale still names the two averages, so nothing is unanswerable).
style.quote_before: When 50-day moving average crosses 200-day moving average, sometimes seen as price 'break out' point.
style.quote_after: A crossover of the short- and long-term moving averages marks a price 'break out' point.

style.detail: Rationale B gained a conflation the original did not have. Option B is about a convergence of the averages and option A is about a crossover; the rewritten rationale now says that a convergence, as well as a crossover, 'is read as a momentum or break-out signal', which blurs the very distinction separating B from the keyed A. B is still false for the reason given (it imposes no requirement to close positions), so the item is not broken, but the added clause works against the item's own discrimination between A and B.
style.quote_before: Incorrect — a crossover signals momentum/break-out; it does not mandate closing positions.
style.quote_after: A moving average crossover or convergence is read as a momentum or break-out signal; it carries no requirement to close open positions.

style.detail: The shortening deleted the exclusivity qualifier that made distractor A false. Before, A was false on its face because of 'only'. After, A reads as a bare statement of an activity the manager genuinely does engage in, and it is wrong only because the stem's 'best described as' frame demands the complete description, which B supplies. The key is still clearly the best of the three and the rationale for A still argues against the cost-only view ('Cost is only one side of the decision'), so this is not mis-keyed, but the distractor no longer fails on its own wording and the discriminating margin now rests entirely on the stem's superlative.
style.quote_before: Setting the hedge ratio requires only minimizing expected hedging costs.
style.quote_after: minimizing the expected cost of hedging.

style.detail: The reframe gave A and B the same verdict, which they did not share in form before. Before, key A carried no recommendation in its option text at all ('Long GBP against HKD; HKD/GBP selling at small forward discount of 0.099% vs current spot...'), so only B asserted 'should hedge'. After, A reads 'advisable, because the forecast loss dwarfs the adverse roll yield' and B reads 'advisable, because the forward discount is the entire cost of the hedge', so the learner must discriminate purely on whether the 0.099% discount is 'the entire cost of the hedge' or merely the roll yield. That distinction is fine in the rationale, but it is weak as the sole discriminator, because the curriculum language retained in the sibling item f_q7 equates the forward discount with the expected cost of the hedge ('the expected cost of the hedge would be 2.5%'). A is still the intended and better answer (its reason is the reading's own reasoning) and B's rationale still calls the 'entire hedging cost' reading wrong, so the item is not double-keyed, but the margin is thinner than before the rewrite.
style.quote_before: Kwun Tong should hedge the GBP exposure because the 0.099% forward discount represents the full cost of hedging over the period.
style.quote_after: advisable, because the forward discount is the entire cost of the hedge.

style.detail: The rewritten stem asks for a method ("The method used to determine the minimum-variance hedge ratio is most likely:"), but option A was re-voiced from an approach into a thing, so the three options are no longer parallel in kind: A is a hedge, B is a technique, C is a quantity. The underlying claim does survive the rewrite -- read against the new stem, "a hedge matched one-for-one to the exposure's notional value" is still the 100%-of-notional assertion, it is still false, and the "after" rationale for A still describes it ("A ratio fixed at 100% of notional is the natural choice for a direct hedge"). So this reads worse against rule 7 but does not break, mis-key or double-key the item. The key (B, "an ordinary least squares regression") remains uniquely correct, and C ("the ratio of the two currencies' interest rates") remains false.
style.quote_before: Approach that always sets the hedge ratio to 100% of the exposure's notional value.
style.quote_after: a hedge matched one-for-one to the exposure's notional value.

style.detail: The key's rationale now asserts, in its own voice, a numeric result about a plan the item never describes. In "before" this sentence sat inside an explicit quotation introduced by "Per the reading:", so the $994 million notional was visibly external worked-example material. Stripping the citation frame (which the spec required) left the figure asserted as if it belonged to this item, but the rewritten stem is the bare conceptual question "The interest rate hedging ratio is most likely a measure of:" -- there is no plan, no asset or liability BPV and no swap BPV anywhere in the item, so "the plan in question" and the $994 million point at something the learner cannot resolve. Not fatal: the stem and all three options are correct and unambiguous, the key is sound, and the dangle is in post-commitment explanation. Fix is to drop "for the plan in question that means entering the receive-fixed swap for a notional principal of $994 million" or recast it as "for example, a plan with a $1,663,080 duration gap and a swap BPV of 0.1673 would enter a notional of about $994 million."
style.quote_before: Correct. Per the reading: 'We use the term "hedging ratio" ... A hedging ratio of 100% indicates an attempt to fully balance, or to immunize, the assets and liabilities. In this case, the plan manager enters the receive-fixed swap for a notional principal of USD994 million.'
style.quote_after: A hedging ratio of 100% indicates an attempt to fully balance, or to immunize, the assets and liabilities; for the plan in question that means entering the receive-fixed swap for a notional principal of $994 million.

style.detail: The rewrite stripped the exhibit reference from the stem but left distractor A as a meta-claim about data that is no longer anywhere in the item, so its subject has no referent. Before, A denied data in a named table the stem pointed at (stem: 'Steepening twist scenario Exhibit 15 most likely:'); after, the stem is the self-contained 'With respect to a steepening twist in the high-quality bond yield curve, it is most likely that:' and A speaks of 'the scenario' that the item never presents. As the item now reads a learner can argue A is literally true (nothing in the stem specifies yields at individual maturities), and A's rationale rebuts it only by citing the 1.5-year/6-year/11.5-year figures that are absent from the stem. Not fatal: B is correct by definition of a steepening twist and remains clearly the best of the three, so the key does not move. But A is now a dead option that points outside the item.
style.quote_before: Exhibit 15 presents no scenario data for a steepening twist.
style.quote_after: the scenario is not specified at individual maturities.

style.detail: This item was legitimately reframed off Equation 6 into a conceptual question, and the key (C, 'the assets and the hedge') is correct and clearly best, so the reframe itself is within the ladder's move 2. The defect is that distractor A was re-voiced to fit the new stem while its rationale was not: A no longer claims that no formula exists, but the rationale still argues against that old claim rather than against what A now says. Rationale A reads 'The relationship is stated explicitly across all three components... Far from there being no such relationship, it is precisely this expression that identifies the sources of risk to a liability-driven investing strategy' — a rebuttal of 'no formula relates these sensitivities', not of 'neither the assets nor the hedge' matches the liability change. The reasoning a learner needs (the equation shows the asset and hedge terms together offsetting the liability term, so 'neither' is false) is present only by implication.
style.quote_before: No formula relates asset, hedge, and liability sensitivities in interest rate hedging.
style.quote_after: neither the assets nor the hedge.

style.detail: The keyed option changed topic. Before, A asserted how index exposure is obtained ('Index-based exposure obtained through traded products.'), a definitional claim about traded products as a route to index exposure. After, A asserts a liquidity ranking ('more liquid than mutual funds.'). That is a different proposition on a different subject, and the stem was rewritten with it ('ETFs for bond market exposure vs mutual funds most likely:' -> 'Bond ETFs are most likely:'). The before item was already self-contained, so the spec's reframe ladder was not available to it ('Do not reframe an item that is already self-contained'), and 'What must not change' requires that 'The correct option makes the same claim it made before, said tersely.' This is NOT fatal: the new A is true on the reading's own words, which the after rationale quotes ('Investors benefit from greater bond ETF liquidity versus mutual funds given the availability of ETF shares to be purchased or sold throughout the trading day'), it is clearly the best of the three, and both distractors remain false (B 'less liquid than the bonds they hold' is contradicted by the after rationale 'ETFs typically offer greater liquidity than their underlying, often thinly traded, fixed-income constituents'; C 'priced once per day at net asset value' is contradicted by 'ETF shares trade continuously throughout the trading day'). The rewrite also buys genuine parallelism, since the old A was a noun-phrase definition sitting beside two liquidity/pricing claims. Flagged so the substitution is a recorded choice rather than an unnoticed drift.
style.quote_before: Index-based exposure obtained through traded products.
style.quote_after: more liquid than mutual funds.

style.detail: The rewritten stem shifts the subject of the duration-drift claim from a portfolio to the benchmark itself. The curriculum point is that fixed-income market dynamics cause a portfolio to deviate from a stable benchmark, one reason being that "the finite maturity of bonds in a static portfolio implies that duration will drift downward over time." A broad bond index does not itself drift downward in duration, because it continuously admits new issuance and drops bonds below its minimum maturity; only a static portfolio held against it does. The item is still answerable and B is still clearly the best of the three (A inverts the direction, C is false on issuer composition), and the phrase "in a static portfolio" carried inside each option is what keeps the claim true, so this is imprecision rather than a broken question. Not fatal, and no fix is being proposed here.
style.quote_before: Fixed-income market dynamics vs equity driving benchmark deviation most likely:
style.quote_after: Unlike an equity benchmark, a broad fixed-income benchmark most likely exhibits:

style.detail: Option C's rationale adds an unsupported causal claim. The source attributes the duration-based yield curve decomposition approach's use in analyst and portfolio manager reports to better transparency at the cost of greater operational complexity (as the 'after' rationale for B itself states: 'exchanging better transparency for more operational complexity'), not to the approach's top-down/bottom-up flexibility. The 'before' rationale for C made no such claim. The option itself is still clearly false and the key (B) is untouched, so this is cosmetic rather than fatal.
style.quote_before: Incorrectly restricts the method; duration-based yield curve decomposition can be top-down or built bottom-up from the security level.
style.quote_after: Duration-based yield curve decomposition can be executed top-down or built bottom-up from the security level, and that flexibility is part of why it is favored for analyst and portfolio manager reporting.

style.quote_before: Benchmark meets criteria of unambiguous (individual securities and weights clearly identifiable), investable (shares freely tradeable), measurable (index returns published daily), reflective of current investment opinions (selected by manager), and specified in advance (not created after fact).
style.quote_after: every validity criterion except appropriateness.
style.detail: The key's claim was broadened from an enumeration of five satisfied criteria to a universal claim over all seven. Bailey and Tierney list seven properties; the before-option asserted only unambiguous, investable, measurable, reflective of current investment opinions and specified in advance, and said nothing about accountable. 'Every validity criterion except appropriateness' now asserts that accountable is satisfied too. Nothing in the reframed stem supports that -- the stem supplies facts only for identifiability, tradeability, daily returns, manager selection and pre-period specification -- and the option's own 'after' rationale still treats accountability as unsettled: 'The manager may still choose to be accountable to this index if the liquidity and capitalization constraints are not expected to interfere with the ability to execute the investment strategy.' So the option as written overstates what its own rationale and the stem's inputs establish, and a candidate who knows accountability is manager-elective can read A as literally false. Severity is style rather than fatal because A remains the only defensible choice against B ('no validity criterion.') and C ('every validity criterion.'), so the item is still answerable and correctly keyed; the fix is to narrow A back to the criteria actually in evidence (e.g. 'all the criteria it can be assessed against except appropriateness' or an explicit five-criteria phrasing).

Rationale C still argues against an interpretive claim the option no longer makes. The before option carried two parts: the inverted formula and an interpretation. The rewrite correctly kept only the formula in the option, but rationale C was left refuting the deleted interpretation, so it ends by rebutting a 'claim' that is nowhere in the item the learner sees. The option is still wrong for the right reason (the ratio is inverted), so the item is not broken; the rationale simply no longer describes the option as it now reads.
style.quote_before: CR = DC/UC; a ratio greater than 1 indicates a convex, positively asymmetric return profile.
style.quote_after: downside capture divided by upside capture. | rationale C: "a value greater than 1 under this inverted form would indicate negative asymmetry, or a concave return profile, rather than the convex, positively asymmetric profile claimed."

style.detail: Rationale B now asserts the opposite of what it asserted before. The before rationale denied that UC - DC measures an average of participation (that was the false interpretation carried in the before option). The after rationale affirms it, saying the difference 'measures the average or net level of participation'. UC - DC is a net difference, not an average, so the rewritten rationale states something incorrect it previously denied. The option itself (a difference rather than a ratio) is still wrong, so the key is unaffected.
style.quote_before: Uses a difference rather than a ratio; the capture ratio is UC/DC and measures return asymmetry, not an average of participation.
style.quote_after: This uses a difference rather than a ratio, and so measures the average or net level of participation instead of its asymmetry.

style.detail: The rewrite added reasoning to rationale A that is not in the before text and is mathematically wrong. For R(B,t) not equal to zero, R(m,t) - R(B,t) = 0 holds exactly when R(m,t)/R(B,t) = 100%, so a zero difference and a 100% ratio always agree at that point by necessity, not by coincidence. The rest of the rationale (a difference does not express the proportion of the benchmark's move captured) is sound, and the option is still correctly wrong, so this is a slip in new rationale prose rather than a broken question.
style.quote_before: Uses a return difference; capture ratios are defined as the ratio of manager to benchmark return, not their difference.
style.quote_after: a difference of zero and a ratio of 100% carry the same message only by coincidence

style.detail: B and C now state the same false proposition in two wordings. After the rewrite, B says a decline is undone by a gain of equal percentage size and C says equal-sized losses and gains offset exactly in cumulative return; these are the same claim, and the two 'after' rationales rebut it with the same argument (the gain is earned on a smaller base). Before, C was about large losses and gains offsetting one-for-one, which read as a distinct claim about magnitude. The key (A) is untouched and both B and C remain wrong, so the item is answerable, but it now effectively offers two options instead of three.
style.quote_before: B: "A 50% decline requires only a 50% gain to recover to the previous value." / C: "Large losses and gains offset one-for-one in cumulative return."
style.quote_after: B: "a decline is recovered by a subsequent gain of equal percentage size." / C: "equal-sized losses and gains offset exactly in cumulative return."

style.detail: Rationale C still rebuts the specific figures the rewrite removed from the option. The option now says only 'a short record' with 'high confidence', but the rationale answers the deleted 'three years' and '90% confidence level', and the trailing clause is garbled English ('far more than a 90% confidence level would be reached on' - years are not more than a confidence level). The option is still false and the key is unaffected; the rationale just no longer tracks the option's wording.
style.quote_before: Skill can be confirmed from three years of outperformance at a 90% confidence level. | rationale C: "may require many years of observations — far more than three — to reach a reasonably high degree of confidence."
style.quote_after: a short record of outperformance confirms skill with high confidence. | rationale C: "far more than three years, and far more than a 90% confidence level would be reached on."

style.detail: Shortening C deleted the clause that made it demonstrably false. Before, C was refutable straight off the stem: it attributed the 17 bps to allocation, while the stem states allocation lost 43 bps. Now C is a bare verdict, and its falseness rests on judgment rather than on a contradiction with the given data - a candidate could argue from this same LOS (returns contain a large element of randomness; many years are needed to confirm skill) that 17 bps over five years is no evidence of skill. A is still clearly the best answer, since the stem asks for the most appropriate conclusion and A is the attribution's own conclusion, so the key holds and I am not calling this fatal; but the distractor is weaker than it was and the broad claim is the kind this pass was warned about.
style.quote_before: Shows no evidence of skill, because the 17 bps of outperformance is entirely attributable to allocation decisions.
style.quote_after: shows no evidence of skill.

style.detail: The distractor's claim shifted from an assumed null of skill to a null of skill already demonstrated, and its own rationale in "after" still describes the old claim. The option now says the test "begins from a null hypothesis of demonstrated skill", while the rationale written for it says "Starting instead from an assumed presence of skill reverses the burden of proof: the manager is hired and retained unless performance disproves a skill that was never demonstrated". An assumed-but-undemonstrated skill and a demonstrated skill are not the same premise, so the rationale no longer describes the option as it reads. Not fatal: the option is still plainly wrong under either reading, since key A carries the no-skill null, and the key stays uniquely correct.
style.quote_before: Manager selection starts from the null hypothesis that the manager IS skillful until performance proves otherwise.
style.quote_after: begins from a null hypothesis of demonstrated skill.

style.detail: The reframe moved the direction of the asymmetry out of the stem and into the options, which was the right fix for the old stem's presupposition, but the result is near-tautological: the stem asks what explains the relative attention and the keyed option answers with "greater concern", which is a restatement of the stem's own subject rather than an explanation of it. The explanatory content now sits entirely in the subordinate clause ("as mistaken rejections cause regret"), so the option partly restates the stem, against the spec's rule that an option is "the candidate answer and nothing else. Not the reasoning, not the arithmetic, not a restatement of the stem." All three options share the defect symmetrically and all three claims are preserved from "before", so the item is still answerable and B is still uniquely correct; this is a readability objection only. A stem such as "Decision makers in manager selection are most likely to give greater attention to:" with options naming the error type would avoid it.
style.quote_before: Why decision makers focus more on Type I errors most likely: | B. Psychologically people seek to avoid feelings of regret — Type I errors are mistaken rejections whereas Type II errors are failures to detect true relationship.
style.quote_after: The relative attention decision makers give to Type I and Type II errors in manager selection is most likely explained by: | B. greater concern with Type I errors, as mistaken rejections cause regret.

style.detail: Option A's claim changed topic from the STATE OF THE RESEARCH to a bare performance assertion, and its rationale still rebuts the dropped qualifier. Before, A was false precisely because of the word 'consistently' — the reading says the evidence is mixed, so a claim that research consistently shows outperformance is wrong on its face. After the rewrite the option asserts only that team-managed funds outperform individually managed funds, which is no longer the claim the rationale answers: the 'after' rationale for A still opens 'The research is mixed rather than consistent', rebutting a word the option no longer contains. Not fatal — the key does not move and B remains uniquely correct (64% of US active mutual funds in 2021 is a majority, so C is wrong, and mixed evidence does not support A) — but this is a per-letter claim change of exactly the kind the audit targets, and it leaves rationale A describing the old option rather than the new one. Note also that A is still non-parallel with B and C (performance vs. prevalence), which was true before the rewrite as well.
style.quote_before: "A": "Research consistently shows team-managed funds outperform individually managed funds." / rationale A: "Wrong: the evidence is mixed — some studies find underperformance, some outperformance, and some no difference."
style.quote_after: "A": "outperform individually managed funds." / rationale A: "The research is mixed rather than consistent: several studies find team-managed funds underperform individually managed funds, several find the opposite, and some find no difference."

style.detail: Option B was shortened from a flat two-part denial to a single clause, and the surviving clause is weaker than the rationale that rebuts it. Before, B asserted both that there is no portfolio-theory analogy and that the finding "stands as an isolated empirical result"; after, B asserts only that the error-reducing mechanism has "no analogue in portfolio theory" — and it now concedes that diversity "Reduces errors," which is true. The after-rationale for B still closes by rebutting the dropped clause ("The finding is therefore not an isolated empirical result"), so it describes a claim the option no longer makes. B is also now arguable rather than cleanly false, because the reading gives a second mechanism with no portfolio analogue (members of diverse teams "may devote more effort to tasks because they are less concerned with socially fitting in"). Not fatal: key A still states the curriculum's exact finding plus its uncorrelated-assets analogy and is unambiguously the best of the three, so the item is not double-keyed. Fix is to restore the isolated-result clause to B or drop that sentence from its rationale.
style.quote_before: The diversity benefit has no analogy in portfolio theory and stands as an isolated empirical result.
style.quote_after: Reduces errors through a mechanism with no analogue in portfolio theory.

style.detail: Rationale C's reasoning is internally awkward rather than wrong. It argues that a 0.50% base fee 'would make the computed fee at least equal to the standard fee at all times, so the breakeven active return would be 0.50% rather than 1.50%' - but if the computed fee never falls below the 0.50% standard fee, every active return at or below 0.50% breaks even, so 0.50% is the upper edge of a flat region, not a single breakeven point. The accompanying cap arithmetic (0.50% + 0.20 x (2.75% - 0.50%) = 0.95%) is correct and the key in slot B is unaffected; this is a wording imprecision in a distractor rationale only.
style.quote_before: Wrong: this swaps the values — the standard fee is 0.50% and the base fee (the floor) is 0.25%.
style.quote_after: A 0.50% base fee would make the computed fee at least equal to the standard fee at all times, so the breakeven active return would be 0.50% rather than 1.50%

style.detail: Letter B's claim was invented rather than shortened. In 'before' the option is the bare fragment "Ethics is defined." - a generator truncation that carries no claim at all. In 'after' it is a specific substantive claim, "compliance with applicable laws and regulations." Strictly this is rule 3 (same letter, different claim). Not fatal: the stored 'before' rationale for B ("Ethics is broader than law; legal compliance is neither necessary nor sufficient for ethical conduct") pins exactly that claim, the reconstructed option is still false, and A ("a set of principles guiding behavior that affects others") remains the single clearly correct choice under the stem "Ethics is best described as:". Flagging only because the content of an option here came from the rationale, not from the option text, so it should be eyeballed by a human rather than trusted as a pure restatement.
style.quote_before: B. "Ethics is defined."  / rationale B: "Incorrect. Ethics is broader than law; legal compliance is neither necessary nor sufficient for ethical conduct."
style.quote_after: B. "compliance with applicable laws and regulations."

style.detail: Option C now carries its own justification inside the option, which house style rule 1 forbids ("An option is the candidate answer and nothing else... If the option explains why it is right, it is wrong"), and it breaks the parallelism of the other two, which are both bare "disclose X" continuations of the stem "...are most likely required to:". The substance is unchanged and the item still keys correctly to B, so this is cosmetic only; "disclose nothing." alone would carry the same claim.
style.quote_before: C. "Completion of the annual Professional Conduct Statement is voluntary and serves only as a reminder of the Code. That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay. Applied uniformly, it would bind at every horizon and every asset class."
style.quote_after: C. "disclose nothing, as completion is voluntary."

style.detail: The rewrite preserves the claim and keeps the option false, so it is not a meaning defect, but the noun-phrase compression produces a fused relative that the learner has to re-read to parse, and it reads as though the Standard 'requires' a transfer. A parallel phrasing such as 'transfer of supervisory responsibility to the person the duties are delegated to' would carry the same claim without the garden path. Flagged only because options A and B in the same item compress cleanly.
style.quote_before: A supervisor who delegates supervisory duties thereby transfers away responsibility for compliance.
style.quote_after: transfer of responsibility to whoever supervisory duties are delegated to.

style.detail: Distractor A lost the qualifier the rationale turns on. Before it claimed permanent recusal from all coverage, with a stated cause; after it claims recusal plainly. The option is still wrong (Standard I(B) requires objective, fundamentals-based analysis, not recusal by the analyst), so the item is not broken, but rationale A still rebuts a permanence claim that the option no longer makes, and the shortening blurs the line against the restricted-list remedy the same rationale cites, which does in practice stop coverage of the issuer.
style.quote_before: A: "Fritz must permanently recuse himself from covering Metals & Mining because the underwriting creates an unavoidable conflict."
style.quote_after: A: "required to recuse himself from covering the company." / rationale A: "Permanent recusal from all coverage of the company is not what the standard requires."

style.detail: The key's hedge was dropped. Before, A asserted only that the recommendation MAY be tainted by a POSSIBLE conflict; after, it asserts flatly that he tainted it. The rationale still carries the hedge, so the option now states something stronger than its own explanation supports. A remains clearly the best of the three (B and C are flatly wrong), and the stem's 'most likely' absorbs some of the loss, which is why this is style rather than fatal; the attribution also shifted from the combination of sponsor-funded travel plus daily access to the president down to 'by taking the trip'.
style.quote_before: A: "his recommendation of Penguin Advisers may be TAINTED by possible conflict incurred when he participated in international trip partly paid for by Penguin Advisers and was in daily company of Penguin's president."
style.quote_after: A: "tainted his recommendation by taking the trip." / rationale A: "his recommendation of Penguin Advisers may be tainted by the possible conflict incurred when he participated in an international trip"

style.detail: The rewritten stem adds a framing the original lacked, and that framing pre-answers distractor A. The stem now asserts the conduct is being assessed under Standard I(B), while A's whole content is that the conduct falls outside the Code's scope; a learner can discard A from the stem without knowing the standard. The original stem carried no such frame. Nothing is mis-keyed and all three options keep their claims, but the item leaks one distractor.
style.quote_before: stem: "Example 11 Mandel: ... outlays handled as ZZYY marketing expenses and disclosed to senior management. Most likely:"
style.quote_after: stem: "Mandel's conduct under Standard I(B) is most likely:" with A: "outside the scope of the Code."

style.detail: All three rewritten options turn on "the standard", but neither the stem nor any option says which standard. In "before", every option named it explicitly (option C: "McGuire violated Standard I(C) because internet site is misleading to potential investors."); the rewrite stripped "Standard I(C)" from A, B and C alike and did not move it into the new stem, which ends only "...without disclosing the contractual relationships with the companies he covers. McGuire most likely:". The key is unaffected and the item is still answerable (C is the only option asserting a violation, and the rationale restores Standard I(C) and VI(A)), so this is not fatal, but the question now asks about an unnamed rule. Fix is to add the standard to the stem, e.g. "...McGuire most likely violated Standard I(C) in that he:", or restore it to one option as q25 does.
style.quote_before: McGuire violated Standard I(C) because internet site is misleading to potential investors.
style.quote_after: violated the standard, because his site misleads investors.

style.detail: Distractor A lost the qualifier that made it coherent with the stem. "Before" said the omission is permitted because the affected account "is only a small portion of assets allocated to outside managers" — a large account that is nonetheless a small slice of the external-manager allocation. The rewrite compresses this to "the account's small share of assets", which now reads as a flat contradiction of the stem's "conceal the poor performance of a large account". The option is still wrong, and wrong for the same reason, so the key does not move; but the "after" rationale for A still argues against the original, fuller claim ("...because the affected account is a small portion of the assets allocated to outside managers"), so option and rationale no longer describe the same proposition. Restoring "of the assets allocated to outside managers" to the option fixes both.
style.quote_before: Scott may omit the change because the affected account is only a small portion of assets allocated to outside managers.
style.quote_after: permitted, given the account's small share of assets.

style.detail: Options B and C now begin "did not violate it", and the pronoun's only antecedent is the text of a sibling option: the stem ends "...although her firm cannot provide tax planning. Rogers most likely:" and never names a standard, so "it" resolves only by reading option A's "violated Standard I(C)." In "before" each option named Standard I(C) for itself. A learner evaluating B or C in isolation has nothing to attach "it" to. Not fatal — the key stays A and the intended reading is recoverable — but the cross-option dependency is a shape the house style's parallel-options rule does not contemplate. Naming the standard in the stem removes it.
style.quote_before: Rogers did not violate Standard I(C) because her assurance was made orally rather than in a written client document.
style.quote_after: did not violate it, because her assurance was oral.

style.detail: Distractor C lost the element that made it false. Before, C asserted a conclusion the rationale refutes: "Because the blog was written with employer permission, no professional-conduct issue arises." After, it reads only "acted within the permission granted by her employer." But the rewritten stem states as given fact that Mewis "writes an ESG blog with her employer's permission", so C now reads as a restatement of a stem-given fact rather than a wrong answer, and its falsity survives only in the rationale ("Permission to maintain the blog is permission to publish, not permission to publish falsehoods."). Key A ("violated Standard I(D) on misconduct.") remains clearly correct and clearly best, so the item is not broken or double-keyed; C is merely a weaker distractor than it was.
style.quote_before: Because the blog was written with employer permission, no professional-conduct issue arises.
style.quote_after: acted within the permission granted by her employer.

style.detail: The rewrite hardened a recommendation into a requirement. The before-item asked only "Client gifts disclosure under I(B) most likely:" and the keyed option carried the guidance's own modal verb: "members and candidates SHOULD disclose to their employers such benefits offered by clients." The after-stem asks what the member "is most likely REQUIRED to" do before accepting, and option A is reduced to the bare act, "Disclose the benefit to the employer." In Standard I(B) the pre-acceptance disclosure is explicitly a 'should' (best practice); only disclosure of benefits already accepted is a 'must'. So as now worded, strictly nothing is required before acceptance, and the after-rationale for A still says so in the guidance's words ("members and candidates should disclose"), which leaves the rationale at odds with the stem it is meant to support. Not fatal: A remains the only defensible choice of the three, since B ("Reject the benefit outright.") and C ("Do nothing, since clients are not third parties.") are both plainly wrong, so the key does not move and the item is not double-keyed. But a careful candidate can object to the stem, and the fix is one word -- 'is most likely expected to' or 'should most likely' in place of 'is most likely required to'.
style.quote_before: stem: "Client gifts disclosure under I(B) most likely:" / A: "Prior to accepting 'bonuses' or gifts from clients, members and candidates should disclose to their employers such benefits offered by clients."
style.quote_after: stem: "Before accepting a bonus or gift offered by a client, a member under Standard I(B) is most likely required to:" / A: "Disclose the benefit to the employer." / rationale A: "prior to accepting bonuses or gifts from clients, members and candidates should disclose to their employers the benefits offered by those clients"

style.quote_before: Monitoring online content under I(C) most likely:
style.quote_after: A member publishes content online and through social media. Under Standard I(C), the member is most likely required to:
style.detail: The rewritten stem recasts a recommended compliance practice as a mandatory one. The source material, quoted in the "after" rationale for A itself, is permissive: "Standard I(C) compliance practices state that members and candidates should regularly monitor materials and content posted online or through social media to ensure that they contain current information." The "before" stem's neutral "most likely:" matched that "should"; "most likely required to:" asserts a requirement the guidance does not state. Not fatal: A ("Monitor the content regularly to keep it current.") is still unambiguously the best of the three, B ("Do nothing further, as the platform assumes responsibility.") and C ("Complete a single compliance review at the time of posting.") remain wrong for their original reasons, and the key stays in A. But a precise learner can object that none of the three is strictly "required," and the fix is to restore a neutral qualifier (e.g. "...the member most likely should:" or "...the recommended practice is most likely to:"), matching how the parallel item r28_prof_los_b_q15 in the same batch handles it ("the recommended practice for avoiding plagiarism most likely includes:").

The distractor lost the qualifier that carried its reason for being wrong. Before, B asserted a permission conditioned on accuracy: cherry-picking is "acceptable if the returns are accurate" — exactly the trap Standard I(C) closes, and exactly what its rationale rebuts. After, the option is reduced to a bare "may represent a strategy", which no longer mentions presentation or accuracy at all. Under the stem ("Standard I(C) most likely holds that:") it still reads as a permission claim and is still false, so the key is not threatened and the item is not broken — but the specific falsity has been blurred, and the rationale now argues against a condition the option no longer states: rationale B still turns on "even where every reported return is accurate", describing the pre-rewrite wording rather than the option as it now reads. Compare the sibling distractor C, which kept its operative verb ("may be presented as factual results"); B should keep its in the same way (e.g. "best-performing accounts may be presented as representative of a strategy").
style.quote_before: Presenting a firm's best-performing accounts as representative of a strategy is acceptable if the returns are accurate.
style.quote_after: the best-performing accounts may represent a strategy.

style.detail: The reframed stem dropped the tipper's name but the rationales still refer to him by it, so the learner reads an explanation about a person the item never introduced. In "before", the name appeared in the stem itself ("Practice Problem 4 Rodriguez/Hart: CFO of Mega Retail tells long-time friend Hart during golf..."). In "after", the stem names only a role ("the chief financial officer of Mega Retail tells his long-time friend Hart"), yet rationale A says "His decision to invest in the retail fund appears directly correlated with Rodriguez's statement about the successful quarter of Mega Retail" and "Rodriguez also violated the standard", and rationale B says "That Rodriguez volunteered the earnings information over a round of golf". Not fatal: the key (A, "violated Standard II(A) by purchasing the retail fund") is still correct and uniquely so, both distractors remain wrong, and the stem supplies every input needed to answer. The fix is to name the CFO Rodriguez in the stem, or to say "the CFO" in the rationales.
style.quote_before: Practice Problem 4 Rodriguez/Hart: CFO of Mega Retail tells long-time friend Hart during golf that quarter will be almost 10% above estimates
style.quote_after: During a round of golf, the chief financial officer of Mega Retail tells his long-time friend Hart that the company's quarter will come in almost 10% above estimates. ... His decision to invest in the retail fund appears directly correlated with Rodriguez's statement about the successful quarter of Mega Retail.

style.detail: The key option's claim was broadened. Before, B asserted a violation by Peter alone and said why; after the reframe of the stem to "Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information is most likely violated by:" it also asserts a violation by the traders, and drops the qualifier the guidance (and the retained rationale) attaches to them - only firm personnel "who are members or candidates" can violate the Code by trading. Strictly, "the personnel who traded" over-claims against personnel who are neither members nor candidates. Not fatal: the reframe required the options to name parties, the proposition is supported by the item's own rationale, and B remains clearly the best of the three (A omits Peter, C clears everyone despite the trading).
style.quote_before: Peter violated Standard II(A) because he failed to prevent the transfer and misuse of material nonpublic information to others in his firm.
style.quote_after: Peter and the personnel who traded.

style.detail: Distractor B lost the universal quantifier that made it false, and its rationale now argues against a claim the option no longer makes. Before, B was a sweeping assertion about interpretive guidance in general ("can never rise to the level of material information"), unambiguously false because the curriculum says such guidance may constitute MNPI. After the reframe the stem became a single fact pattern ("A company privately gives an analyst guidance interpreting its already published financial statements. That guidance is most likely:") and B became the bare predicate "immaterial" about that one instance. Nothing in the new stem says what the guidance contained, so B is no longer false on its face -- it is merely not the curriculum's point -- while key C now asserts flatly that the guidance IS material nonpublic information where the source only warns analysts to "be alert to the possibility" that it is. The key is still the intended and best answer, so this is not fatal, but the margin over B now rests on exam convention rather than on B being wrong. Compounding it, the "after" rationale for B opens "Interpretive guidance can be material" and goes on to say interpretation "may itself constitute material nonpublic information" -- i.e. it rebuts the deleted "can never" universal, not the option as it now reads.
style.quote_before: Interpretation assistance from investor relations can never rise to the level of material information. That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay. Applied uniformly, it would bind at every horizon and every asset class. No cycle overlay would be allowed to lift or cut that bound.
style.quote_after: immaterial.

style.detail: The reframed stem drops the old citation header that supplied the actor's name and opens anonymously, then refers to him by name in the lead-in, leaving 'Clement' with no antecedent. Still answerable (he is the only individual in the stem, and 'He retains his support material and changes his rating on Turgot Chariots' pins the reference), so readability only. Separately, the stem generalized 'APAC currency analysts' / 'KRW depreciation' to 'regional currency analysts' / 'currency depreciation' while after-rationale C still itemizes 'the margin pressure from depreciation of the Korean won' — the rationale is now more specific than the stem it explains.
style.quote_before: Example 6 Clement/Turgot (mosaic theory): senior automobile analyst speaks with reps, salespeople, labor leaders, APAC currency analysts, banking officials
style.quote_after: A senior automobile analyst speaks with company representatives, salespeople, labor leaders, regional currency analysts, and banking officials. ... Clement most likely:

style.detail: The adverb 'knowingly' moved and now modifies the wrong party. In 'before' it qualifies the member's engagement in the conduct, which is the standard's actual formulation; in 'after' it qualifies the inducement ('conduct that may knowingly induce'), which is not what Standard II(A) says and is incoherent on its own terms — conduct does not induce knowingly, a person acts knowingly. The scienter requirement attaches to the inducement rather than to the member. Not fatal: A ('only inducement for which the insider is compensated.') and B ('only a direct request for the information.') are both still clearly false, and C is still plainly the best answer, so the key holds and is unambiguous. The after-rationale for C restores the correct phrasing ('must not knowingly engage in any conduct that may induce company insiders to privately disclose material nonpublic information'), so the rationale no longer matches the option as it now reads. Fix is a one-word move: 'any conduct that may induce such disclosure.'
style.quote_before: Members and candidates must NOT knowingly engage in any conduct that may induce company insiders to privately disclose material nonpublic information.
style.quote_after: any conduct that may knowingly induce such disclosure.

style.detail: Distractor B lost the MNPI qualifier to a demonstrative with no antecedent in the rewritten stem. Before, B named what the agreement asserted: "stating no MNPI will be conveyed". After, it is "agreements that no such information was conveyed", but the rewritten stem says only "information through an expert network" and never mentions material nonpublic information, so "such information" points at nothing and B reads as agreements that no information at all was conveyed. The claim is still false for the same reason and the key in A is unaffected, so this is not fatal; it reads worse. Fix would be "rely on the participants' agreements that no material nonpublic information was conveyed."
style.quote_before: A signed expert-network agreement stating no MNPI will be conveyed fully protects the receiving analyst.
style.quote_after: rely on the participants' agreements that no such information was conveyed.

style.detail: Before, C was a flatly false claim about METHOD: suitability is assessed issue-by-issue. After, C is a verdict with a method clause attached, and read literally as a conditional ('unsuitable, IF judged position by position') it is arguably true rather than false — a covered call viewed in isolation can look wrong for a risk-averse client. Its wrongness now depends on the reader taking the trailing clause as an endorsement of the prohibited method rather than as a premise. Compounding this, A and C now return the SAME verdict ('unsuitable'), distinguished only by the reasoning bolted onto each, so the item offers two answers rather than three. Not fatal: key B is the only option saying 'suitable', so the key still stands alone and rationale C still rebuts the position-by-position method ('Judging each option position in isolation is the opposite of the required approach'). But the distractor is weaker than the one it replaced.
style.quote_before: Suitability is judged option position by option position, without reference to the rest of the client's holdings.
style.quote_after: unsuitable, when judged position by position.

style.detail: The reframed stem drops the Example 5 framing and introduces the account as 'The IPS of Gubler's client' with '4% of the portfolio'. Rationale A, lifted verbatim from the curriculum comment, still speaks of 'the subsidiary's assets' — a party that no longer exists anywhere in the item. The learner reading the explanation meets a subsidiary the question never mentioned. Substance and arithmetic are intact (three-year lockup, laddered exit to five years or more, highly-liquid mandate); only the orphaned noun is wrong. Rationales B and C were correctly re-voiced to the new framing ('how small the allocation is', 'the three-year lockup and the laddered exit'), so this is an inconsistency within the after text itself.
style.quote_before: Gubler violated Standard III(C); new investment locks up part of subsidiary's assets for at least 3 years
style.quote_after: The new investment locks up part of the subsidiary's assets for at least three years and up to as many as five years or more.

style.detail: The rewrite adds a setup fact that was not in 'before': that the policy statement 'permits the use of ESG factors'. The before stem described the IPS only as 'family office IPS focused on long-term capital preservation and downside risk mitigation'. The LOS point being tested is precisely that a manager MAY incorporate criteria beyond financial metrics; stipulating that permission in the stem lets the learner reject option C ('violated the Standard by letting non-financial criteria influence suitability') from the stem alone, without knowing the guidance. Rationale B then leans on the stipulation ('the use of ESG factors is permissible under the mandate'), content absent from the before rationale, which argued from the general permission instead. Permitted under reframe move 1 only in the sense that nothing became wrong: the key does not move and no distractor turns true. But the item now answers itself, which is a weaker question than the one it replaced.
style.quote_before: family office IPS focused on long-term capital preservation and downside risk mitigation; considers Park (better financials) vs Dong (higher ESG scores)
style.quote_after: Kim manages a family office whose investment policy statement emphasizes long-term capital preservation and downside risk mitigation and permits the use of ESG factors.

style.detail: The stem's fourth composite defect was de-fanged: 'manipulates accounts included in composite over time' became 'has its membership changed over time', and membership changing over time is ordinary composite maintenance, not misconduct. Rationale A still says 'its membership is manipulated over time', so the rationale describes a fact the item no longer states. Not fatal: key A remains clearly best on the undisclosed sub-asset-level exclusion and the inclusion of accounts lacking a balanced mandate because they help results.
style.quote_before: includes accounts that do NOT have balanced mandate (because they help results), and manipulates accounts included in composite over time
style.quote_after: includes accounts that do not have a balanced mandate because they improve the results, and has its membership changed over time

style.detail: Shortening the key removed the only place the item said the composite was ever shown to anyone. Standard III(D) is a performance-presentation standard, and both rationale A ('misrepresenting the facts in the promotional material sent to prospective clients') and rationale B ('sending that record to prospective clients is a misrepresentation under Standard III(D)') turn on a promotional presentation to prospective clients that now appears nowhere in the stem or options. Not fatal: the stem names Standard III(D) and option C's "'unaudited' label" still implies a client-facing report, so the learner can reach A.
