style.quote_before: Kilmer violated Standard III(D) by misrepresenting facts in promotional material sent to prospective clients, distorting his firm's performance record, and failing to include disclosures that would have clarified the presentation.
style.quote_after: violated the Standard by distorting the firm's performance record.

style.detail: The distractor lost the qualifier that made it a plausible trap. 'during that one year' is what made the premise true but insufficient; 'the growth figure reported' points at the brochure's claim of 'consistently achieves 25% annual growth', which the stem shows is not accurate, so C's own premise is now contradicted by the stem rather than being a tempting half-truth. Rationale C still argues against the old wording ('The one-year figure is literally accurate, which is what makes the answer tempting'), describing a claim the option no longer makes. Not fatal: C is still wrong and key B is still the only defensible answer.
style.quote_before: There is no violation because the fund did in fact achieve 25% growth during that one year.
style.quote_after: complied, because the growth figure reported is accurate.

style.quote_before: When uncertain about the right course, the member should proceed unilaterally on professional judgment alone.
style.quote_after: act on his or her own professional judgment.
style.detail: The shortening drops both words that carried the falsity, "unilaterally" and "alone". What is left, "act on his or her own professional judgment", is a weaker claim: exercising professional judgment is not itself contrary to Standard III(A), so the option now reads closer to a half-truth than to the clearly wrong statement it was. The key (C, "consider what he or she would expect as the client") is still the verbatim compliance practice and still unambiguously the best of the three, so the item is not mis-keyed or double-keyed and I am not calling this fatal. But the option's own rationale still describes the stronger version it no longer makes: "Proceeding unilaterally on professional judgment skips both the client's perspective and the written disclosure and approval that the practice calls for." Restoring one qualifier (e.g. "act on his or her own professional judgment alone") would put the option back in step with its rationale.

Borderline, not fatal. The rewrite made C parallel to B by giving it the same conclusion plus a different reason, so B and C now both assert a violation and the item discriminates only on which reason the curriculum endorses. Before, C was a bare non-parallel classification claim that did not assert a violation at all; after, it reads as a competing correct conclusion, and the proposition it rests on (CFA Program registration and exam fees are not research) is itself true. B remains the better answer and is still clearly keyable: the after-C rationale carries the before version's own disclaimer that classification 'is not the determining issue' and that the violation lies in 'the direction of the benefit'. Per-letter claims were preserved (rule 3 is satisfied) and the substance of the collision pre-existed the rewrite, so I am not calling this mis-keyed or double-keyed - only flagging that the parallelism pass sharpened the weakest discrimination in the slice.
style.quote_before: C option: "CFA Program doesn't meet research definition."  (B option: "Stafford violated the Code and Standards because improving her investment skills is not a reasonable use of the soft dollar account.")
style.quote_after: C option: "a violation, because the program is not research."  (B option: "a violation, because the benefit is personal.")

style.detail: The rewrite moved the standard's name out of the options but never put it in the stem, so all three options now refer to an antecedent-less "the standard." In "before", two of the three options named it explicitly (A: "Claudius violated Standard IV(C) solely by assigning both portfolios to a single manager." / C: "Claudius violated Standard IV(C) by failing to adequately supervise Tabbing with respect to her S&P 500 trading."). In "after" the stem ends "Claudius most likely:" with no standard cited anywhere, and the options read "violated the standard by the dual assignment alone." / "did not violate the standard." / "violated the standard by failing to supervise the futures trading." The item is still answerable (only one option describes the conduct correctly, and all three concern the same unnamed standard, so the key is not in doubt), which is why this is style rather than fatal; but the learner is asked about a standard the question never identifies. The sibling items in this slice do it correctly - q22's rewritten stem keeps "With respect to Standard IV(B), Hollis most likely:" and q27's option C keeps "violated Standard IV(C)." Either naming the standard in the stem or keeping it in the options would close the gap.
style.quote_before: Claudius violated Standard IV(C) solely by assigning both portfolios to a single manager.
style.quote_after: Claudius most likely: ... violated the standard by failing to supervise the futures trading.

style.detail: Option C changed topic: it was about needing employer approval to ADHERE to the Code and Standards; under the new stem ("With respect to giving an employer a copy of the Code and Standards, members and candidates are most likely:") it is now about needing approval to GIVE the employer a copy. The 'after' rationale was expanded but still rebuts the old claim, not the option as it now reads: it argues that adherence is never conditioned on employer approval, which answers a proposition the option no longer makes. Not fatal - the option is still false as rewritten and key B ("encouraged to do so") remains uniquely correct, so the item is neither mis-keyed nor unanswerable - but this is a substantive claim shift plus a rationale/option mismatch, not a cosmetic one.
style.quote_before: Members and candidates must obtain employer approval before adhering to the Code and Standards. / rationale: "Wrong - adherence to the Code and Standards is mandatory and is never conditioned on employer approval."
style.quote_after: required to obtain approval first. / rationale: "Adherence to the Code and Standards is a condition of membership and candidacy and is never conditioned on an employer's approval."

style.detail: The rewritten B rationale argues around a fact the rewritten stem no longer contains. In "before", the fund-returns detail lived in option B itself ("since the meeting centered on fund returns"); the rewrite reduced B to the bare label "Performance Presentation." and moved the detail into the rationale as a concession ("even though returns featured in the presentation"). But the "after" stem says only that Hockett and Lopez "take them through a presentation and explain why a balanced portfolio is best suited to them" — nothing about returns. The rationale therefore rebuts a reading of the item the learner cannot have had. Not fatal: key A is still correct and B is still wrong. Fix is to delete the trailing clause.
style.quote_before: B (option): "The failure is one of performance presentation under Standard III(D), since the meeting centered on fund returns."
style.quote_after: B (rationale): "nothing in the meeting suggests performance was misstated, even though returns featured in the presentation"

style.detail: The qualifier that made this distractor false was deleted. In "before", B located the failure in Corrales's own objectivity when selecting the subadvisers, which is clearly not the tested violation. The rewrite leaves a bare standard name, and against the rewritten stem — Corrales pays undocumented "deal fees" to buy "close connections with high-ranking local officials" to "facilitate governmental support" — the bare label is no longer plainly false: Standard I(B) prohibits offering any benefit that could reasonably be expected to compromise ANOTHER's independence and objectivity, which is a fair description of bribing officials. The key's own rationale concedes "Such conduct violates multiple standards". Judged style rather than fatal only because the "after" B rationale re-imposes the missing qualifier ("not a compromise of Corrales's own objectivity in selecting the subadvisers"), so the distractor is still described as wrong for its original reason, and C remains the best answer under "most likely". Restoring the qualifier to the option would remove the ambiguity.
style.quote_before: B: "The failure concerns independence and objectivity, since the officials' connections influenced the selection."
style.quote_after: B: "Independence and Objectivity."

style.detail: Same mechanism on the other distractor: the single word "only" was the falsifier and it is gone. "The failure is one of diligence and reasonable basis only" is unambiguously false; "Diligence and Reasonable Basis." is not, because the stem states Corrales hires subadvisers with "minimal investment experience" and "does not require details of the activities those fees pay for", and this repo's sibling drill r35_appl_los_b_q4 states that "investment advisers who hire subadvisers must ensure they have the necessary knowledge or expertise to meet the need for diligence and thoroughness" (/home/user/CFA/CFAL3/Resources/los_drills_r35.json:1245). Style rather than fatal for the same reason as the B finding: the "after" A rationale still carries the exclusion ("it is not what this item turns on"), and C is the standard the case solution names.
style.quote_before: A: "The failure is one of diligence and reasonable basis only, since the subadvisers lack investment experience."
style.quote_after: A: "Diligence and Reasonable Basis."
